utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Monday, July 6th, 2009, and I welcome first Mr. Praljak. I apologise to Mr. Praljak for having forgotten his name last week. I must have been thinking about the other accused. Well, I also greet Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Stojic. I also greet all the Defence counsels, Mr. Stringer, Mr. Scott, and their assistants, and of course I greet our Registrar, our usher, our court reporter, and of course our interpreters and security guards. I don't think I forgot anyone. If I did, you know, you could raise your hand. Well, no one is raising their hand, so it seems everyone's been included. Let me read a short oral decision. Oral decision on July 6th, 2009, on the letter sent by Accused Jadranko Prlic to the Judges of this Trial Chamber. On July 4th, 2009, sent a letter to the Trial Chamber in which it seems that he's asking for the Trial Chamber to review its decision of June 29, 2009, called "Decision on a Request by the Prlic Defence to Review the Decision on the Admission of Evidence." The Trial Chamber reminds the accused Prlic, as well as his counsel, that the only avenue allowed to challenge such a decision is to make a request for certification of appeal, filed in due form by the counsels of the accused. That was the oral decision. We were also informed by the Registrar that Mr. Prlic decided to attend the hearings, and the Trial Chamber is quite happy about this. Mr. Prlic will come into this courtroom after our first break, because he's on his way and we only were told about the fact that he wanted to attend about ten minutes ago. So he'll be with us after the first break. I think I understood that Mr. Karnavas had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Prlic had made his decision to come as a result of my conversation with him on Friday, based on the Trial Chamber's decision with respect to ADC, a decision which was filed -- it was an order, as I understand. It was filed on a confidential basis, although I do believe that for the sake of transparency, these sorts of issues should be held in open public. But for those reasons, Mr. Prlic will come here, and at that point in time I will address the Court, prior to Mr. Prlic taking the floor, to express his given position. Unless you want to hear my position at this point in time, but I would prefer for Dr. Prlic to be here so he can listen to it as well. And I should also note that on my way into the building, I stopped in at the ADC to see whether they received anything. It appears that nothing has been received by them. And I would also add, as having been the former president of the ADC, that the order is misdirected. What we're actually asking for is an advisory opinion from the Disciplinary Council. That's where the order should be directed to, and not the Amicus Committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll be waiting for Mr. Prlic after the break, and you will take the floor when he will be in the courtroom. Ms. Alaburic, I believe that you have a few minutes left, and now you have the floor to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good afternoon to you and everybody else in the courtroom. I think I still have some ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General Praljak, I suggest we deal with Mostar. How far we're going to go, we'll see in these ten minutes. Anyway, good afternoon to you, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom, and good afternoon to you, too, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On Thursday, we left discussing the shelling in Mostar and the fighting there, and I'd like to round off that area with just one more question. Tell me, please, did the HVO have observers who observed and supervised the firing of certain mortar shells or any similar artillery action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, depending on the information sent back by the observers, were corrections made in shooting, in conformity with the rules of warfare in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next topic relating to Mostar is an allegation made in the indictment that I'd like to address by which the separation lines that we've discussed a great deal in this courtroom, and I assume we're all well aware of that, are the result of the conflict on the 9th of May, 1993. So tell us now, please, General Praljak, is that right or was that separation line established on some other day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The separation line was established earlier on, while General Pellnas was doing the mediation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Pellnas, during his testimony in this courtroom, said that that separation line was set up based on an agreement reached in the night between the 20th and 21st of April, 1993. And that was recorded on page 19760 of the transcript. Tell us now, please, General Praljak, to the best of your recollections, was that the date of the separation line and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and I took part with General Pellnas in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General Praljak, I'd like to ask you something about three documents that are to be found at the end of the second binder in the section titled "Mostar." And you will be able to find the documents on your screen. They'll be called up on e-court. 4D1344 is the first document. And while we're waiting for that to come up on our screens, tell us, General, you did mention some Muslim-Serb agreement, did you not, which was reached in the conflict in Mostar on the 9th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it was that you talked to us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge and information, an agreement was signed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm very unpleased that I have to do this again and again. Please kindly wait for the question, and then wait and pause and then answer. So it is -- I believe that it is not so difficult to understand this and to act accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General. You started your answer. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am just waiting for what we've said to come up on the screen. Now, according to the information I had at the time, and it was public in a way -- well, yes, it was publicised, that an agreement had been signed between Ratko Mladic and Sefer Halilovic on the 8th of May, 1993, about a cease -- immediate cease-fire throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina between the BH Army and the Army of Republika Srpska on the other side. Now, the witness was General Philippe Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, please look at the document. 4D1344 was the number, and it is an agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, just a minute. The document we have here on the screen, in which General Morillon obviously is a witness - he's a witness very often - well, it seems that this is a cease-fire agreement between Halilovic and Mladic, between the Serbs and the Muslims. Now, I'm looking at the date, May 8th, 1993. I'm sure you know that May 8th, 1993, is just a day before May 9, and because of this, I have a couple of questions that come to mind. If Mostar was actually attacked by ABiH and not by the HVO, which is the case that you've been putting forth since the inception of this trial, I say if the ABiH is not even allowed to -- not allowed to attack against the HVO, they might as well be quiet with the Serbs in the meanwhile, and so there could be a reason for having a cease-fire with the Serbs, with a witness that can be instrumented, i.e., General Morillon. Then the Serbs are no longer doing anything, and the Muslims have -- are entirely free to the attack the HVO. Is this possible or is this pure speculation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, it's not guess-work. They signed the cease-fire on the 8th with the Serbs, and I claim that they attacked the HVO in Mostar on the 9th. And similarly in September, they signed a complete cease-fire with the Serbs, and then they directed the fiercest part of the Neretva-93 offensive toward the HVO. So that wasn't the first time, nor was it the only time, to ensure their rear and to sign an agreement with the other side without asking General Petkovic or the HVO or them taking part as the regular army. So this kind of one-sided cease-fire agreements were to the detriment of the third party always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, from your answer just now, I can conclude, can I not, that the document we have up on our screens is precisely the agreement between Mladic and Halilovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's go on to look at the next document, which is 4D1345, and that is a document which represents the operationalisation or implementation of the agreement between Mladic and Halilovic, and the order was issued by Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd Corps. And here for that area of responsibility, based on the agreement that we'd mentioned a moment ago between Mladic and Halilovic, an order is being issued on the cessation of all combat operations against the Army of Republika Srpska. Tell us please, General Praljak, did you know that it was on the basis of the Mladic-Halilovic agreement that orders were issued for individual areas of responsibility of the corps to cease combat against the Serb Army? Can you comment on the contents of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is logical. That is what was done, and I did know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now let's move on. We're going to skip a period of time and deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you know, I try to integrate all the documents that we see and try to tie this up with what happened on the May 9. Obviously, this document, which comes from the 3rd Corps, is obviously implementing what we saw on the previous document, but there could be another assumption, which is the following, and I'm going to tell you about this idea, and I would like you to tell me what your position could be. Let's say that -- actually it's the Prosecution's case, which is right, and it is the HVO which attacked the ABiH, but that the intelligence service of the Serbs and of the Muslims found out about the HVO that was getting ready for an offensive. I mean, there is military intelligence going on at the time. So if the HVO -- if suddenly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if the ABiH learns that the HVO is going to attack, they might say, Well, we might as well mobilise our forces against the HVO and not the Serbs. Then they decide on May 8th to sign an agreement, the cease-fire agreement, because they've obtained intelligence a few days earlier about a possible attack of the HVO. Now, is this totally ludicrous or is this -- do the elements that you had from the field, can they grant this hypothesis or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's not a single element, Judge Antonetti, which would confirm that hypothesis. Quite the reverse, in fact. You have seen documents dated to April 1993 in which the BH Army has a completely elaborated military plan of attack against the HVO in Mostar, and that plan was quite obviously not implemented, in part due to my involvement and General Pellnas's involvement, who invested every effort to prevent an attack by the BH Army at that point in time, and they wouldn't have been able to carry out the attack in front of him, with him there. And, secondly, my transfer to East Mostar was an element in that it wasn't a logical move, in view of the fact that there was great tension all around, and the fact that I sat down to drink a cup of coffee with Mr. Pasalic and went to the SDA party, asking them -- asking people there who were still not supporting a conflict to come out into the town and state their views. But obviously the Military Section, together with Sefer Halilovic at its head, implemented its plan on the 9th of May. Now, hypothetically, your assertion, I suppose, could be taken as being possible, but there was no element -- no HVO plan to attack on the 9th of May, no previous order or elaborated military action, no troops were brought in, or anything else that would support that either on paper or through a witness. It's not a simple operation to carry out, so it would have needed a great deal of preparation. So I claim, once again, that after the 9th of May, after the agreement was had been signed with the Serbs, it was the BH Army which attacked, according to all the information I had and all the discussions and talks I had up until that date and later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, and I believe it's important. The agreement signed between Halilovic and Mladic on May 8th, witnessed by the international community, represented by the famous General Morillon, okay, this cease-fire is well known, so if the ABiH attacks the HVO, didn't the international community -- wasn't the international community instrumented by the ABiH, were they duped, because, on the one hand, the ABiH is pretending to have a cease-fire, but, on the other hand, it's getting ready to attack the HVO and actually attacking the HVO? What's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said this many times already, and I will again. Regrettably, the international community, primarily because of the situation in Sarajevo, accepted any information from the BH Army indiscriminately, without even meaning to look at the facts. It was for that reason alone that inaccurate information was being conveyed throughout, and that is why the HVO was accused. You saw Mr. Drekovic's book which talked about the lines against the Serbs to the north and south of Mostar, and he called those lines mere guard posts, described them as being at that level. If the VRS was the arch-enemy of the BH Army, which would have been logical, whereas the HVO, an army which based on all documents and principles and pure reason should have been a partner, that it's impossible to explain why they would have set up mere guard posts facing the VRS and never, ever took any action whatsoever in that direction; not only in that area, but nowhere at all, not in terms of the corridor, not in the direction of Srebrenica, and so on and so forth. I have said this a number of times already. I'm still waiting to be refuted. Mr. Halilovic, in his book, claims that Neretva-93 operation was the one major real offensive ever launched by the BH Army against its partners. He had 200.000 men, and the big question is what he possibly would have achieved fighting the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's look at the following document in relation to the 30th of June, 1993. The document number is 2D1389, 2D1389.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And whereabouts is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's right after this one, in the same section. I do have to skip some documents because I have reorganised my cross-examination a little.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ones coming up next are all marked as "4D."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One of them should be 2D1389, but there we have it on our screens. Page 2, please, of the Croatian, the last paragraph on page 2 in the English. The last paragraph on page 2 in the English. This document is entitled "Information on the Course of Conduct Activities on the 30th of June," put together by the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces in Sarajevo. The paragraph is entitled "Area of Responsibility of the 4th Corps." It reads as follows. Simply because it's very significant, I will be reading the entire paragraph. I quote: "Our forces successfully repelled yesterday's attack by Ustasha units and captured some very important strongholds in a counter-attack, Sjeverni Logor, Rastane, Vrapce, Bijelo Polje, Salakovci and Rosci. Among other things, we hold all the hydroelectric power-plants along the Neretva River, except for the one in Capljina. About 100 soldiers surrendered to our forces, and several hundred captured civilians have been freed. The BH Army seized a large booty consisting of weapons and ammunition in the North Camp. "Based on the report of the 4th Corps Command, the units yesterday linked up with the forces of the 6th corps, which will have a favourable effect on any further progress of combat activities." End of quote. General Praljak, can you confirm the accuracy of this report, to begin with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What's inaccurate about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of the BH Army reports, as evidenced by the journalist who was in charge of covering Neretva-93 operation, start off on a false note. The Ustasha forces attacked us, and then we launched a counter-attack, that was false. Therefore, with the exception of this very first sentence, that the Ustasha - and that was us, that's what they called us - without holding anything back or any reservations whatsoever, this was a vial, sly, underhanded, treacherous attack, not just by the BH Army, but also by the Muslims within the HVO. It was a synchronised attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, let's try to interpret the meaning of the last sentence for the benefit of the Chamber. The 6th Corps, which area of responsibility would that be or which geographical area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jablanica-Konjic, and then the surrounding areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about the 4th Corps, which area would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Mostar area. Those two corps, following this operation, linked up along the Basta Bijelok [phoen] road which they had controlled up until that point in time. Many stories about Mostar's isolation and being besieged have no basis in facts. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, based on your information, after that day what about the BH Army in the Mostar area? Did they keep receiving assistance, in terms of manpower, ammunition, and weapons, unhindered from Jablanica and further into Bosnia and Herzegovina, further inland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was the military depot in Visoko which we kept replenishing. That particular depot kept furnishing the 4th and the 6th Corps with weapons incessantly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Two brief questions about my own client, General Petkovic. General Praljak, you said that at the time that you were the number-one man of the Main Staff. There was an internal distribution of tasks under which General Petkovic was in charge of Central Bosnia, contacts with the international players, and the commanders of the Muslim and Serb armies in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that a fair summary of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Needless to say, when he was there, he had a task, but then he was also given a special task to press on with the talks, because he had been in charge of that earlier on as well. He did a brilliant job in each and every way. And then he had a special task of looking after Central Bosnia. The focus of his work, as one normally puts it, was to remain in Central Bosnia. To the extent that he could, he was in charge of keeping Kiseljak alive, in particular, as well as trying, doing his best, to link up with Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You say that Mr. Tole was particularly in charge of the Mostar area, he was the chief of the Main Staff in your time; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was counter-intuitive for the BH Army to score a success in Mostar and in the south without previously taking Uskoplje and Rama, Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, and then further south towards Vrde, in order to reach Mostar and the right riverbank from behind. That is why I took over that particular area, because according to military logic, this was the most fervent -- difficult area, whereas Mr. Tole got a special assignment to look after Mostar and its south. That was an internal division or distribution of tasks that we had. I'm talking about what the focus was for each and every one of us. If I headed south and I was involved in the fighting there, then obviously I was the one taking the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, given the fact that my time is running out, I have one final question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your time has already expired by already five minutes, so all the time that will be devoted will be taken down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, one final question. When you told us about how, on the 30th of June, 1993, a total, all-out war broke out between the BH Army and the HVO, my question is an attempt to clarify the following: Did this all-out war occur precisely because of the linking up of the 4th and 6th Corps, resulting in a possibility that enormous forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from Central Bosnia, might be caught up in defensive [as interpreted] activities towards Mostar and further south towards the Adriatic coast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a military viewpoint, that is correct. Units from the 1st Corps could have been dispatched there and added to the existing forces, and this was exactly what was being done. Nevertheless, Ms. Alaburic, the most difficult problem we were facing was the HVO psychology. Up until that point in time, we had held out hope, to some extent, to the effect that there would be no all-out war and that they would not get what they were driving for. Regardless of how many elements were opposing this opinion, the hope was still alive. After the treason by their own men within the HVO, the most important element caved in, what we refer to as the moral backbone in men. The men there felt betrayed not just by the BH Army but in part also by their own leaders, who throughout this time and despite their justified assurances that the BH Army were up to something, and we actually knew this ourselves, we were all adamant, nevertheless, that there should be an amicable approach, that the weapons should be handed over to them, that there would be no clashes erupting and so on and so forth. And this was something that was much more difficult to deal with than the military aspect, which of course allowed the BH Army, for three or four months, to go on with their offensive all the way from Bugojno in order to eventually reach the Adriatic coast, thereby resolving the Serb-Muslim problem within the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I thank you for your answer. And, Your Honours, if I may just correct the transcript. Page 14, line 23, it's about to disappear off our screens, I was talking about the offensive activities of the BH Army towards Mostar and down towards the Adriatic coast, whereas the transcript says "defensive activities." If it was a slip of the tongue on my part, I do apologise. Your Honours, I thank you for the extra time I have been granted to cross-examine General Praljak. Thank you very much for your kindness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Judges have been faced with two cases, the one from the Prosecution and the one from the Defence, every time that I get a document with a military origin, I'm trying to look at this document and to see how it compares with your case and the case from the Prosecution to try and understand and to reach the truth. In the document that we have before us, which is coming from the ABiH, it says that the aggressor, namely, yourself, the Chetniks and the Ustashas, it says that you use seven tanks as well as some armoured vehicles to attack the town of Zepce. If this document is true, you are not in a defensive operation, because you have always said that as far as the HVO was concerned, they were defending themselves and they were never attacking. But what this document states is that you were the attacking party and in quite substantial means, with seven tanks and other armoured vehicles or armoured carriers. Therefore, you're not in defensive mode, all the more so because, according to this document, you ask for Zepce to surrender. So as far as you can recollect, has there been an attack in Zepce with seven tanks and some sufficient means to carry out this attack, or do you feel that this document is not reflecting the current situation of then to justify their own behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is entirely inaccurate in terms of the information that it offers. Zepce was entirely surrounded by the BH Army. The 111th Zepce Brigade did not have seven tanks, no way. These are bare-faced lies, which is something that happens in a war. But the truth was this: Zepce was surrounded on all sides. It had no contact with any other unit, with the exception of that brigade that was surrounded by the BH Army throughout. It was far away from any other source of support from the HVO that it might have received. They were attacking Zepce constantly, and every time after an attack, they would say, The HVO launched an attack to which we responded by a counter-attack, and so on and so forth. Zepce was surrounded, suffering heavy, enormous losses. It could hardly do anything else but defend. There was no possibility of a breakthrough. Anyone to link up with was far too far away. There was nothing at all, no avenue that was open to them. I could show this to you on a map, but I believe you know this already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the expense of my own time, just a single question which I think might be helpful, in terms of clarifying this particular answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The question is: General Praljak, the Zepce area, was that a Croatian enclave in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and those people fought bitterly to not be wiped off the face of the earth, such as Vares and Kakanj. And they actually succeeded. They only had a small area to go on. They were suffering enormous losses, and they did it. Seven tanks, come on. Not even a ten-year-old child would buy that story. We were barely able to dispatch some infantry weapons, small arms, to them, and RPGs for them to defend themselves with. Again, we had to do this across Serb-held territory, which we had to pay for. Needless to say, the VRS saw it as being in their best interests for the BH Army and the HVO to clash. That is why they allowed us to use their territory, and we paid them in money and in fuel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will give the floor to the counsel of Mr. Coric. But before I give him the floor or give her the floor, I would like to advise you that the Registry has informed me that Mr. Prlic has arrived, so he will join us after the break. I should also like to inform Counsel Karnavas, who is going to take the floor later on, in order to avoid any mistake, because he was talking about a disciplinary procedure, I would like to remind Counsel Karnavas, given that you wanted publicly to touch upon this issue, that in a decision that was handed down by the Chamber, it was said in the preamble, and that I will mention immediately in order to avoid any mistake, it said: "Whereas the Chamber was wondering on the accountability of such a behaviour of the Prlic Defence, in conformity with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Code of Ethics; whereas the Chamber feels necessary to have the opinion of an amicus curiae ..." So the Chamber is still looking into the case. And in order for this thinking to come to fruition, we have asked for an opinion from the amicus curiae. So there is no disciplinary measure that has been decided upon as yet. Very well. So we are now going to move to Mr. Coric's Defence. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to you, too, Mr. Praljak, and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the usher to hand out the binders, I'd like to deal with two technical matters. I have four hours and forty-five minutes at my disposal for my cross-examination. However, to avoid any time constraints and pressures, and at the request of my client, Mr. Coric, I wanted to ask the Trial Chamber to give me equal opportunity as they afforded to the Petkovic Defence; that is to say, that if I don't complete my cross-examination within that time, that I can use the Coric Defence time allotted. I do, however, think that I will be able to end my cross-examination within the four hours and forty-five minutes, but I just wanted to request that. The second point has to do with the binders. Everybody has been given three binders, that is to say, the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution, and the witness, and we'll start off with the small, thin binder which actually looks like this [indicates]. That's what we're going to start off with. I'll take a moment and wait for all the binders to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar is handing out the various binders. I would like to know whether there are three binders, including a small one, and then two red ones; is that correct? Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Precisely, Judge, and we're going to start off with the small one, because I'm going to move on to another larger area, whereas we'll be able to get through the small one, I hope, by the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first question for you, Mr. Praljak, has nothing to do with the binders and documents, but is linked to something that you said when questioned by Ms. Alaburic. And in view of everything that you said on direct, I think that there was a slight misunderstanding at one point, and I'll tell you -- I'll put it to you, what you said, and you can tell us whether that is what you actually thought and wanted say and whether it's a misunderstanding. Asked by Ms. Alaburic, and the question was recorded on page 42427 of the transcript and 42428 of the transcript, whether the SIS, the military police, and the IPD were established as parallel systems to exercise political control, and I emphasise "political," political control over the army, your answer was in the affirmative. Now I'm going to ask you this one again. Was there a misunderstanding or do you claim that the military police was established in order to exercise political control over the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police did not exercise political control over the army, nor did the SIS exercise political control over the army, nor again was political control exercised over the army by the IPD. And even with parallel systems, I explained in quite exact terms what is meant by a parallel system, so I don't think that there can be any misunderstanding on that score. Let me state again, there was no political control from the head of the Military Police Administration or whatever you like to call him.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. Now, my next question relates to a document shown to you by Judge Antonetti, and I think that it was one that was put to you during the examination-in-chief. It is P01350, and it is the first document in your binder. I'd like to read something out from that document. It is the fourth paragraph from the top, and that paragraph begins with the following words: "From the proposal made by the chief ...," and it says: "In Gornji Vakuf, the military police had the task of protecting the military police of the area, the population, and securing safe traffic. That task was soon expanded to include the following in the chief's absence, but everybody recognises that the military police bore the greatest burden and the greatest sacrifices." Now, Mr. Praljak, these are the minutes from a meeting, and I think that you said that you attended at least part of that meeting, so I'd like to know whether what I have just read out was the truth and whether you were aware of that. Do you happen to remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend this meeting for a time, in part, and, well, there were a lot of questions that were raised, and I took the floor. It is true that the military police took part in the fighting in Uskoplje, as far as I know. I wasn't the commander of that particular operation, so I don't know about all the details. I was just there. I was there to be in the final stages of that operation. But as I've said loud and clear, I did not have -- now, whether I could have is another matter, but I did not have the possibility and opportunity to challenge the arguments put forward by the commander of that particular action about the fact that it was necessary after the BH Army had fully blocked the HVO in Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, do you remember that this is what was stated at the meeting, the portion I read out and quoted? If you can't remember, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, madam, rest assured that that is what I'll do. But I can't remember, so that's my answer. It's been a long time, and I don't know whether I left after making my speech. That was probably it. I probably did go, did leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. Now let's look at another document, 5D0054 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, when I have a military document, I always look at it and I make an analysis, putting it back into the context. And sometimes the document provides very informative details. On page 4 of the English version, there is Mr. Petrovic that is taking the floor. Several people seem to take the floor. And General Petrovic talks about the importance of the team from the guard on duty or the officer on duty, and he says that he has to be aware of the entirety of the situation on the theatre, and this has to be done at all times. Could you please confirm that when there was a military operation, what happened, necessarily, was that you had a duty officer or an officer following up the military operation, and this officer had to be informed in realtime about everything that was happening on the ground, on the theatre of operations? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I be of assistance with the terminology? I don't think that the interpreter had the Croatian version in front of them, but we're talking about the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is the duty operations officer. So, General Praljak, was there always a duty operations officer who was accounting in realtime about the situation? He was informed and then he would feed back the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With more important operations, there was the duty officer, but unfortunately the information that came into him in realtime was very scant and not sufficient, either no information at all or very scant information. And the reasons for that was that the lines of communication were in a terrible state: There was no proper communication on the ground between the individual units, the commanders of operations, or the axes of operations, and they had to make due with -- well, I can explain what they used and why the system wasn't actually functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's not really what I'm interested in. I'm going to go back to the 9th of May. Let's take on board the case of the Prosecutor; namely, that it is you, the HVO, who is attacking. If there is an HVO attack, and it means that you take over the headquarters of the BiH, which is not a small matter, do you think that if that was the case, you had a duty operations officer within the headquarters who had written down on some document, of some log, 5.00, this and that, 10 past 5.00, this and that action so and so, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. When you have a very important operation, then you had to have all the information, a complete plan, the beginning and end of an attack, the sign given to launch the attack, the artillery and how it was going to be deployed, when you had managed to take control of a certain area, and so on and so forth. And you were able to see from June 1992, Your Honours, the two documents that I provided. When information of that kind comes in, it comes in every two or three minutes, giving an update. This happened here, Praljak said that, ordered this. So it was a very dense log-book that you had to keep, because information was coming in all the time when any major operation was underway. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, let's look at the next document, which is 5D00548, and it is a document that is already an exhibit, and we've seen it several times in this courtroom already. It was signed by Mr. Coric, and it is titled "Request for Re-Examination of the Engagement of Units of the Military Police on the Front-Lines." There's no need for us to read through the entire document. I'd just like to read the first paragraph and the last three paragraphs. Here is what it says: "On several occasions, we have warned, and we are doing so by this request as well, that the Administration of the Military Police, due to intensive and non-stop involvement of the units of the military police on the front-lines, and also due to the impossibility of replenishing the units with new troops, it is unable to perform the military police tasks according to its competence." Now we can move on to the last three paragraphs, the end of the document: "Terror and crime of all kinds is on the increase and, therefore, worrying, and threatens that on the free territory of the HR-HB, that it will lead to anarchy and lawlessness. "I hereby announce, with full responsibility, that the military police forces which remain after the units of the military police have been deployed to the front-lines, we will not be in a position to perform even our regular military police tasks, let alone the complex interventions and other significant military police tasks. "Because of the above, we demand that there be a re-examination of the involvement of the military police up at the front-lines, and we suggest that the military police units should be withdrawn from the front-lines so as to be able to carry out military police activities and that only -- that they be sent to the front-lines only in exceptional situations." Now, Mr. Praljak, I recall that during the examination-in-chief you confirmed that you were aware of this particular problem. Am I right in saying that; is that right? Did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, madam. I was informed of this problem, and I fully subscribe to what it says here. I would put my signature at the bottom of that document in the place of Mr. Coric. And this document, in fact, illustrates what I said on many occasions in this courtroom, and that is that after the attack on the 9th of May, and especially after the 30th of June, in military terms and, to a certain extent, in the moral sense, the HVO system disintegrated, I mean the people, the population, everything, so that Mr. Coric is quite right when he says that deploying the military police units considerably reduced their possibility to do their proper job. But I followed a different logic. That's the only thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, well, we'll come to that, Mr. Praljak, in due course. You do remember that Mr. Biskic testified in this court, don't you? At transcript page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, just a minute. Before we go into Mr. Biskic's testimony, let me go back to this document. I'm discovering it, actually, 5D00158. General Praljak, a few years -- a few months ago, even years ago, I wondered why there was so many casualties among military police people. We've seen a number of documents where we noted that there were a lot of casualties and fatalities, and I was very surprised by this. Now, here in this document, it was written by Mr. Coric, this problem is actually mentioned. He says that if the military police is placed on the front-line, then it will be exposed and there will probably be casualties, which is why he's mentioning them. But he's saying something else which is extremely important, as far as his liability under Article 7(3) is concerned. He says the very fact of placing these military police people on the front-line, because of this there is an increase in terror and crimes, and chaos reigns, as well as anarchy. So he's obviously blowing the whistle. I'm sure that you haven't read the entire case law of the Nuremberg trials. There is case law, but it has to do with the responsibility of generals in occupied territories. Unfortunately, the jurisprudence is not extended to the combat zone. But at least in the case law we have from the Nuremberg trial, the general in charge of the occupied territories is responsible of absolutely everything, everything, from A to Z, including order in the streets and including all crimes that may be committed in the streets. And, obviously, here Mr. Coric is telling you about this, since you are a recipient of this letter, as well as Mr. Tole and Mr. Stojic. So when you have this kind of military report, when you obtain these kind of military reports, what measures did you take to help Mr. Coric and to make sure that the military police went back to its own traditional job and only that, or did you not do anything because you had no seasoned fighters and you only had these military policemen at hand, and they were -- at least they knew how to handle weapons, they were disciplined, they obeyed orders, and at least they made it possible for a defence to be carried out? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies, but let us try not to confuse the general. The figure that was entered was not accurate. You asked for 5D50048 [as interpreted], and the one in the transcript is "158." I don't think the general really knows which to be document to be looking at. 5D00548, that's the correct document number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The correct document is the one you mentioned earlier, 5D00548. General Praljak, can you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Not only is it a fact that 30 years ago I read a lot of those documents and some important books on the Nuremberg trials, moreover I was, for different reasons, an avid student of these chaotic states of human society in my capacity as a sociologist, and that was the case more than once. As for a general's responsibility in this occupied territory, there was no occupied territory in my case. There was fighting along the front-line. Secondly, when we do encounter occupied territories, there are vast differences between an occupation by a structured, well-organised army and the forces sufficiently competent to maintain order, on the one hand, and the chaos, on the other, that ensues when a war is in the process of being lost or a battle is in the process of being lost, be it the escape from Moscow, in Napoleon's case, or the escape from Moscow in World War II when everyone was smashing things up, and stealing, and so on and so forth, be it following Katherine or Katrina. In this case, Your Honours, I was aware of the problem, but there were two options -- two avenues that were open to me. One was to return the military police to Mr. Coric and for the BH Army to reach the Adriatic coast. There were no more than two options. These were splendid fighters, 39 killed, 191 seriously wounded. They were holding their lines and fending off any attacks. At these most difficult times, that's what I was talking about. At a time like this, I took a decision which I still recognise as my own today. I made a request and obtained a signature from Mate Boban entitling me to use military police for operative tasks, simply because that was the military situation that prevailed at the time. As soon as the situation was sorted out, the military police went back. I assert, Your Honours, that everything that we can read in the indictment is not there because the explanations in the indictment are what they are, but rather because the offensive launched by the BH Army was a fierce one, fearful. Even worse, there were drawn-out negotiations underway, and on top of that the Muslim treason in the area. People reached a stage known as the decomposition of the moral backbone. In a way, we have been deceiving them and convincing them that something entirely different was, in fact, the case, but then the people, who had been saying all along that this would eventually occur, ended up saying, There, see, they attacked us eventually, they are double-dealing, they betrayed us, same as back in 1944, history repeating itself. There were a lot of independent players, so to speak, there were free shooters emerging in a situation like this, and the pressure exerted by the BH Army, in the military sense, was such that the military police as well as components of the civilian police had to get involved, as well as each and every human beings in that area. I stand by my decision. It was exactly the course of action to be taken in a situation like that. As for those who committed any wrongdoings in a situation like that, there will always be time later on to bring those men to face justice. Had I returned the military police there to do their job, they would have been left without anything to do, simply because we would no longer be -- we would no longer have remained in that area. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is precisely what I was trying to say what Mr. Biskic said when he testified. In his evidence -- well, let's not waste any time quoting all the transcript pages, but it's there for all to read, Mr. Biskic's evidence, and he said that the country's defence was the top priority. It was perfectly normal and necessary for the military police to get involved and in the way just described by General Praljak. He also said that after he took up his position there, he asked the then chief of the Main Staff, General Roso, to issue an order to withdraw the military police units from the front-line, and also confirmed what Mr. Praljak said, that it was eventually done, except he said it was done sometime in mid-December 1993, when the conditions were finally ripe for a move like that. I was trying to ask further questions to get there, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You're testifying. You're testifying, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. I'm sure this is why Mr. Stringer is on his feet. You should rather say, Mr. Biskic says this and that, and General Praljak can confirm. Mr. Stringer, is this what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In a sense, yes, Mr. President. I understood that counsel was repeating what she was saying was the testimony of Mr. Biskic, and I'm not doubting that, but I was going to request that counsel give the page numbers of the transcript because I might go back to read that later, and it would help me find it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page, please. Would you please give us the page, please? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'll provide the page numbers. First, what I was trying to say is that my questions were to follow. I was going to talk to General Praljak about this, and ask him if he remembers this, Mr. Biskic saying that, whether he agrees with what Mr. Biskic said. And, of course, I can first ask the question and afterwards I can proceed and give you the pages numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Of course I remember. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Page numbers from the transcript are 15181, 15186, 15242, 15261, 15265, 15267, 15274, 15279, 15282, and 15309.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let us please move on to the two last documents in this binder, the first document being P03117. This is an order by the commander of the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, Brigadier Miljenko Lasic. The date is the 2nd of July, 1993. The order is addressed to two HVO brigades, a military police battalion, the Operative Zone Logistics Section, the sector commanders, and yet another addressee, ONOZJIH. Probably you'll know what that stands for, but I don't think it's of any relevance at this point in time. The order reads, and I'll just read the sentence before the word "order" itself: "With respect to the duties to be carried out in the Central Zone of Responsibility, the Mostar Defence Zone, I hereby order ..." And then the zones of responsibility are defined. What I'm looking at is paragraph 2, reading: "The zone of responsibility shall be divided into three sectors ..." And then a list of these sectors. So this is the second zone of responsibility. Under paragraph 2, the second zone of responsibility: "I hereby appoint Mr. Mijo Jelic sector commander, who is also the commander of the military police." If we look at paragraph 4, it reads: "Daily reports, in a written form, reflecting the situation as at 1800 hours are submitted by sector commanders on a daily basis by 2000 hours. Telephone reports are to be submitted by 730 and 1700 hours. Interim reports are submitted as required or as dictated by necessity." A single question in relation to this document: Mr. Praljak, were you familiar with that? Were you aware of the fact that Mr. Mijo Jelic was appointed commander of the 2nd zone of responsibility in Mostar in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, madam, I wasn't there on the 2nd of July. I did know that Mr. Mijo Jelic had been appointed commander of the city of Mostar by an order signed by Tolic, chief of the Main Staff, but it wasn't until at a much later stage that I actually saw the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us try to move on to the later document, P03983. The document is dated the 6th of August, 1993. As you have told us, this is about the appointment of Mr. -- of Mr. Jelic as the defence commander of Mostar. Paragraph 2 reads: "All of the units in Mostar are hereby placed under the command of Mr. Mijo Jelic." Further, regulating a request -- or, rather, a proposal to set up a staff or a headquarters, how reports will be submitted on the implementation of this order. You told us a moment ago you knew about this; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: Thank you very much, Mr. Praljak. Your Honours, I'm looking at the clock. I'm about to move on to a rather substantial topic. I would like to take the break now, if possible, because I wish to attain a certain degree of continuity covering that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we will have our 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The court is back in session. The Trial Chamber welcomes Mr. Prlic. I believe that Mr. Karnavas has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon again, Mr. President, Your Honours. On Friday, we received the -- I believe it's titled "Order" that was submitted to the Association of Defence Council practicing before the ICTY, known as ADC, which is our professional association, with an order/request to the Amicus Committee. It appeared that the order was requesting what we consider or what other Trial Chambers have considered as an advisory opinion, an advisory opinion based on a factual setting which, quite frankly, and with all due respect, I find to be incorrect and somewhat misleading, because it doesn't lay out all of the facts as we presented. So there are some factual issues. But be that as it may, based on what we were able to glean, and that when I say "we," I speak for Ms. Tomanovic, we came away with the impression that the Trial Chamber finds these two lawyers to be unethical, unprofessional, deceitful towards the Trial Chamber, and that, I categorically, along with Suzana Tomanovic, we categorically deny these allegations, as they seem to be framed in the questions as put by the Trial Chamber. At all times, we've acted professionally, ethically, conscientiously. At all times, we have been consulting with our clients. At all times, we did what we thought was best under the circumstances. And as I indicated in my supplemental submission, we were provided documents on the basis that we would abide by the requests of the sources. We will have ample time to address those issues. I will be asking the ADC to request from the Trial Chamber to make its findings based on the record, the entire record, or, in the alternative, to ask the President of the Tribunal to select three Judges for an independent and impartial panel of Judges to determine the facts in order to determine whether, indeed, this particular team has acted in an inappropriate manner. I'm also going to be requesting the ADC to consult with leading experts in the field of ethics and professional conduct, primarily from the adversarial system, since we are engaged in an adversarial system, and presumably these experts would be able to provide and edify us with the responsibilities of Defence lawyers in conducting investigations on behalf of their clients in an adversarial setting. Based on what we read, I was quite concerned, as was Mr. Tomanovic, and so I went to see Dr. Prlic on Friday, between 6.00 and 8.00 p.m. It was our concern that in light of what it appears are, from the reading of -- and we're going through our unofficial translation, but we have good interpreters and translators. It appears that we no longer enjoy, if we ever did, any credibility in front of this Trial Chamber. And in light of that, I informed Dr. Prlic that it may be in his best interests if I were to come to court and ask that the proceedings be suspended until such time as this cloud is lifted over our heads. Ms. Tomanovic and I are fully confident that we have not done anything illegal, improper, unprofessional, and that we will be cleared, but we are concerned that henceforward whatever we do or say, and perhaps even in the past, in light of the Trial Chamber's findings from the facts as it puts it, that we are deceitful lawyers, and in that -- given that, we are not able to plead his case and conduct our business in his best interests. So I suggested that we suspended the proceedings. The alternative would be to ask the Registrar to appoint independent counsel to represent him during this interim period and for us to withdraw or step aside until such time as this matter is cleared. Dr. Prlic is of the opinion that the trial should continue. He's also of the opinion, which I do not particularly share, but this is his opinion, that he is fully capable to take over, in a sense, any questioning in the court very much as General Praljak has done on numerous occasions. As I understand it, he will be addressing you, but we fully enjoy his support and his confidence. He wishes for us to continue in our capacity as his lawyers and to assist him, but until this time, until this sword of Damocles, if you want to put it, is lifted from our heads, Mr. Prlic is suggesting that he be permitted to act as his counsel in court for the purposes of asking questions to the witness while we continue in our capacity to draft motions, do the research, do everything that we normally would do, except we would not be necessarily either objecting or be making any pleadings in the court. And in light of the Trial Chamber's timetable, and in light of the upcoming break that we have, and the fact that we have already cross-examined General Praljak, it would appear that during this interim period there would be little to do as far as in-court presentation on behalf of Dr. Prlic, who of course we would be -- we would be assisting. But in any event, my concern was for this. I did at one point suggest that I withdraw completely from the case, because my interest is his best interest. And if the Trial Chamber thinks, and I put it to him very bluntly and very crudely, it appears the Trial Chamber sees his lawyers as "sleazy," this is how I put it, this is how I interpret this, that somehow we are less than honest with the Trial Chamber. This is the very first I've ever been called by the Trial Chamber to answer to anything with respect to these sorts of allegations as I find here today, and I find them extremely serious and extremely regrettable. So, in any event, our position is that the matter be suspended until such time as we clear this issue. Dr. Prlic has other opinions, it is his case. However, I advise against him representing himself, even during this interim period, but I am in your hands, as well as he is in your hands, and he is here and he is prepared to address the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll give the floor to Mr. Prlic, but I believe that there's -- you make a small mistake, Mr. Karnavas. It's not the ADC and amicus curiae. In its decision, the Trial Chamber asked the ADC to play the role of amicus curiae. It's a single entity. There isn't two entities; there's only one. Secondly, the Trial Chamber, having noted a potential technical problem, is requesting the ADC for its enlightened opinion. In the decision, we gave them one month, we gave the ADC one month, to give us its technical point of view on three issues. I'm almost sure -- I don't really know how the ADC works, but if I refer to the practice in other states, the ADC will take a look at the problem, might appoint a rapporteur, and then will come to you for explanations, and then will give us its enlightened opinion on these three questions. Right now, the Trial Chamber is wondering about many things, is asking for advice, is trusting the ADC. We could have asked someone else, you know, to give us an enlight ened opinion, but we wanted to call on the best specialists for this, and they will give us their enlightened opinion, their advice, telling us, There is no problem, There is a problem. I don't know what they'll say. As of now, we are in the dark. We're waiting for the enlightened opinion of this -- and this informed opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I understand that. As I've indicated, the manner in which we see the facts as being presented, and the facts which are -- the questions are predicated upon, which we find to be incomplete, give rise to a different opinion from our perspective. But be that as it may, if I may be of some assistance, given that you're asking for an enlightened opinion concerning ethical behaviour, the ADC has, within the various committees, has a disciplinary council, and in the past they have provided advisory opinions which have assisted Trial Chambers in resolving issues such as conflicts. I believe that was the primary one that comes to mind at this point. So you may wish to redirect that. And, furthermore, as I've indicated, as of today they have yet -- the ADC has yet to receive your decision or order or request, so you may wish to have someone from the Registry provide that to the ADC so they can act as expeditiously as possible. But this is our reading of it, Your Honour, and I don't want to take up any more time, but we do take grave exceptions to some of the characterisations that are being made here, and we do believe there are issues of fact as well, which is perhaps why we are concerned that we no longer are able to do our job on behalf of Dr. Prlic, because we're here for him. We're not here for ourselves, and the moment that we are here as an obstacle and not as a benefit to one of the -- to our client, it's time for us to step aside. I mean, that's my professional responsibility, that's how I see it. It's not about money, it's not about ego, it's not about reputation; it's about the client. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prlic, I will give you the floor. Let me tell you that, personally, I'm very glad to see you back in the courtroom, and I hope that you will stay with us. You have all the information at hand. The Trial Chamber has issued a decision. I'm sure it was translated into English and probably into B/C/S also. In this decision, it is said that the Trial Chamber has asked for advice from the ADC on three technical issues, and we're waiting -- we gave the ADC one month to provide us with their advice, and then we will see how to proceed later on. Now, given this, Mr. Karnavas just told us this morning that you would attend the hearing this afternoon, we've heard Mr. Karnavas now, and he told us that you wanted also to give your opinion. So now you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Thank you. I haven't seen you for a while. I'm going to address a few issues, and I've prepared what I want to say. And if you want to give it to interpreters, this is going to make their life easier. [Interpretation] I'm here today because of this newly-arisen situation with respect to my Defence counsel and my Defence team as a whole. I'm here to try and find a solution so that the trial does not suffer. I don't want a spot of blemish to be on my Defence team, and nothing that is not founded on the highest ethical criteria. Now, at the same time, since Judge Antonetti raised a number of issues, Judge Prandler also intervened, allow me to respond to them. My request has been very simple from the very beginning, and that is that I have a proper and correct trial, and I stated this on several occasions. When my Defence case was completed and when I saw that during those proceedings I did not have a role to play, I simply ceased to come into the courtroom, not only without having uttered any bad word, but without uttering any word at all. I did not want to impede the proceedings that evolved without me and suffered no major problems because of that. When I was not able to do anything else, I resorted to silence, I chose silence, and the prison to which you convicted me without a conviction, because at the end of the Defence case I asked to be allowed to be provisionally released until a judgement was reached instead of having no judgement and remaining in prison for another two years. For two years, even if only for -- two years, if only for procedural issues, is not -- no little time. And before that, I had not missed a single second of the trial in court, either during the Prosecution case or during my Defence case. Therefore, I showed every respect for the Trial Chamber and for the Tribunal, and that is why I do have the right to speak about this Tribunal, more than anybody else in this courtroom, regardless of my position at this point in time. I do not earn a living from it, as opposed to other people in this courtroom, with the exception of the accused, of course. So it is in my interests that this Tribunal functions and functions properly. You have your records. You can see that I always supported the ideas and ideals of this Tribunal from the very beginning in 1993, right up until the indictment. I even supported it when it was dangerous to do so and when one was considered a traitor if one did support it, and even when it became quite clear that it wasn't achieving the role it set out to achieve. I signed the peace agreement in Dayton, and part of that agreement was cooperation with the Tribunal, as a member of the state delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I represented that country and its victims in the world for more than five years. I attended sessions for six years of the General Assembly of the United Nations, and for the most part I spoke about the importance of this Tribunal, the meaning it has, and I took part at the Rome Diplomatic Conference about the establishment of a permanent international criminal court. Dozens of times in interviews, I stated that I would always respond if the Tribunal asked me to do so. And on the same day when the indictment arrived, and it was handed to me in Zagreb and not in Sarajevo, where it also arrived, but it was intentionally not handed over to me there when I was actually in Sarajevo, I handed myself over and came here straight away, and that is why I want this Tribunal to be a success and that there should be no trial which should not be shown to be efficacious and credible. And I am conscious of the fact that there is going to be collateral damage, the damage I'm suffering myself already. Now let me respond to some of Judge Antonetti's questions. Judge Antonetti says that I perhaps consider that the trial is a farce, a mock trial. Now, bearing in mind the character of the indictment itself and how the entire proceedings were organised, instead of a direct answer at this point in time, I'm going to resort to a sentence that was uttered in Brussels during our last conversation before he was killed, a sentence used by Zoran Djindjic, the prime minister of Serbia, and I quote: "When you hop on to the wrong train, then all the stations are wrong stations." And let me say that I have always presented my views. On the 21st of March, 2007, for instance, I said that I did not wish to take an active part in the trial because I considered the indictment to be unjustified, and I feel it to be in an adverse position when I have to justify myself and respond. And I think raising an indictment of this kind is a great error on the part of the Prosecution. Although I received information well ahead of time that I would be indicted, that information reached me in Tehran, Iran, in 1994. And I asked where the information came from, and I was told, We are controlling all that. Whatever I asked for from this Trial Chamber, I was refused. I was refused a laptop, and the Registrar even agreed, when talking to me, that it was no problem for me to be able to use a laptop during the court proceedings. I took the floor in this courtroom several times, but nothing happened. For example, I made a request for additional time to examine a few of the Prosecution witnesses, Tomljanovich, Manolic, Okun, Galbraith, and a couple of those from protected organisations. On the 16th of April, 2007, I made another request. I asked that we should not be treated as a group by you. Judge Antonetti last week, on Thursday, in actual fact, said on page 42304 of the transcript, that you were very generous in allotting time for cross-examination and that that, in the Karadzic trial, will only amount to 60 per cent. I agree, had I had 60 per cent and had the Prosecution had 60 per cent in their examination, which of course is not the case. The Prosecutor has 100 per cent, and I don't mind, I have nothing against that. My Defence team has just one-sixth of that. I also requested a separation of trials and I was refused, a severance. And I spoke about the problems of adjudicated facts, which challenged the credibility of this entire proceedings, and I addressed the matter of agreed facts as well, and I spoke about the problems of the documents and evidence that the Prosecution had. I also spoke of the trial itself and said that my Defence counsel was using only 10 per cent of the questions I suggested that he ask or the material he tendered into evidence, in addition to other things, to prove the following: Whose JCE it was and who supports that joint criminal enterprise today. Now, let me remind you that on one occasion, I asked an IC number for a certain document and some time calculation, and that certain portions of these proceedings should not be done in private session, should not be confidential. None of that was -- I was not allowed to do any of that. My requests were rejected, and, finally, in addition to my statement, after which I left the courtroom, although before you rejected our requests, we had decided to request provisional release to the end of trial. As I've already said, the decision to make a statement was taken just a few days prior to the beginning of the Defence case, bearing in mind your decision about the time allotted to the Defence from the 25th of April, 2008. You know that I publicly gave up on my right to an expeditious trial. I publicly renounced that right in order to give the Prosecution enough time for whatever it deems necessary. And that implied the same for my Defence, too, but I received almost nothing in return. The time requested for my Defence case was only partially permitted. But that's gone by, too, and we didn't complain, we didn't object, because we were conscious of the fact that the Appeals Chamber would change nothing, and that is indeed what happened. Nothing changed. Therefore, I decided to go ahead with an introductory statement that I prepared during the seven days of provisional release that you allowed me to take last year, and not with my testimony, so that within the time allotted, the other witnesses, who had already been scheduled, could be examined and present their testimony. So we used up all the additional time, and it was no easy matter to plan our time. And, Judge Antonetti, you were able to see that during the examination and cross-examination of General Praljak. Yes, I wrote in -- a response to the Tomljanovich expert report, and as I said last year, several hundred pages, with 1.500 footnotes. All the accused here watched me writing this over a period of many days. And I wrote a response to the expert report on the presidential transcripts as well. That was a lengthy response, too, with 1500 footnotes again, but you did not accept that expert report, so that I wasn't able to put forward that part of what I had prepared. And let me just add that I also wrote responses to the expert report by Professor Ribicic, and I suppose I will have to leave that for some later date in a book I might publish. I'm saying this to tell me you that I did intend to take part in these proceedings indirectly, and not directly through questions and answers and the like, because, after all, that's why I have my Defence counsel. The annex which you rejected, I could have read out here in the courtroom today, just as I'm doing now, and taken up a week of court time. So it's not only a week; it's actually a million dollars. I decided to save the UN the expense of that million dollars, and as opposed to you, who took the decision to use that same million and continue our stay in prison during that time. I did not ask you to give any weight or relevance to my response to the expert witness report, just to read it instead of listening to me. It's up to you, what weight you give to it. But you said that you did not even wish to read it. I understood that. I understood that as saying that you weren't interested in it. So you gave precedence to form rather than substance, whereas you accepted evidence and you're using it, and you accepted the aggressive discussion in the same tone that this man Tomljanovich used in his dealings with me. I informed one of my Defence counsel with response to your request with respect to his unethical behaviour. He wants to clear this matter up in principle, and he has all my support on that score. He also informed me, and I'm conscious of the fact, that there is fear, that people are afraid of this institution, unfortunately, and some people don't want to have anything to do with this Tribunal. Once again, I say "unfortunately so," but their request must be respected. Their respect for anonymity must be respected. However, throughout the subject of documentary evidence, this is not important, bearing in mind the fact that all the documents have been asked to be reconsidered and, therefore, receive proof of authenticity by those who were ready to do so publicly. Since I have gone through all those documents, I can say that they are very trivial documents, just like hundreds of others that have been admitted into evidence here. My Defence team has no hidden agenda except to ensure a fair and just trial. And my Defence counsel put forward two variants; one, to interrupt the trial until all these questions are resolved, because, as he said, he considers that in the meantime, but to the end of these proceedings, my Defence, bearing in mind all your requests, is losing on credibility, part of its credibility, or to appoint a temporary representative. None of these two options are acceptable to me, and I told him so on Friday night. I don't want this trial to be interrupted. I don't wish the court proceedings to be interrupted. I wish to be part of the solution, not part of the problem. And a new representative, I don't think that is realistic. So I don't wish the trial to be suspended. Now, whatever happens, with all the variants put forward, it is always I who am going to have to pay the bills, and I made another proposal. In looking for a solution, I looked at the Praljak example. Perhaps I could take part in the proceedings, ask questions, give answers, perhaps at the beginning of September until the request is resolved. We are coming up for a summer recess, and looking at -- we are in the course of General Praljak's cross-examination, so I don't expect my Defence team to take any more significant role in the trial at this stage. Of course, the proceedings will continue, but I would intervene if the need arises. I sincerely believe that I won't need to do so, because my Defence team have already completed their job. I am proposing this, and I think you will find that acceptable, because I don't wish the credibility of my Defence team to come into question at no point, and I would like to repeat that. I have to return to the question posed by Judge Antonetti, do I believe that this trial is a farce. What is one supposed to think about the fact that seven years after entering prison, one is still waiting for a first sentence to be issued in the trial, the main problem in the entire proceedings being a shortage of time? Take my word for it, I'm unable to explain this to anyone who might bother to ask. You have all the records showing what I did and in what I was involved throughout my career. I do possess certain knowledge and certain experience. Believe me, all of this could have taken no more than a couple of months if there had been a logical interdisciplinary procedure. One cannot pose complex social, economic, demographic, political, financial, international-law-related, sociological, national and historical questions and deal with them in a procedure that is envisaged for a criminal trial, no matter how good that procedure is. This is simply impossible. I said once, while agreeing with a comment made by Judge Trechsel on page 17110, I quote: [In English] "Since it is not possible to establish the truth, I am not participating in the trial." [Interpretation] Judge Prandler has shown that he knows a lot about the region. As for how Bosnia and Herzegovina functioned, a single example suffices: The visit of your own boss -- I'm not sure if you were a member of the ministry at the time - the foreign minister, Laslo Kovac, his visit to Sarajevo in 1994 or 1995. Hungary was presiding over the OSCE at the time, and it was followed by Switzerland. This was a point in time when I worked with Minister Flavio Koti, it's just that I wasn't sure about the exact year, 1994 or 1995. At the end of the meeting, Kovac, in occupied Sarajevo at the end of this meeting, as a token of assistance from his government, gave us a package containing 60.000 marks in cash. What follows from that was that there was no domestic currency, there were no functioning banks, and there was no communication. There was no nothing. There, this explanation has taken under a minute. We've resolved that, and we are now free to move on. That would be my style, roughly speaking. If we only look at these questions and other -- a more than well-known questions, such as the country's economy, the currency, the cash-flow, we've lost months and months of work in our time in prison on these issues. I would like to say a couple of words now about documentary evidence, which is a key issue.
