Judge Antonetti, at the beginning of Mr. Praljak's cross-examination, explained that he had accepted the wording of the indictment in early March, 1994, when confirming the indictment in a very formal way. You said this -- you see that I'm reading the transcript, although I'm not physically present at the trial, at pages 41359-41360. And then my own documentary evidence was refused, again for purely formal reasons, as it seemed to me. During the Prosecution case, one must constantly bear in mind the fact that the onus is on the Prosecution, or at least that's what we were told. You will be bringing your own evidence during the Defence case. But then Rule 98 bis was applied to take into account only Prosecution evidence and not any Defence evidence, which, in my opinion, makes no sense at all. That is why we did not file any 92 bis motion. Had the situation been different, had we been given sufficient time for our cross-examination during the Prosecution case, and had the request to acquit been considered during that stage, following all the evidence that had been tendered and admitted, I am deeply convinced that no defence would have been necessary at all. At least we would not have been adamant that we should have a defence. Then our time was reduced for Defence, and we submitted a request for documentary evidence, all of them of course from the 65 ter list, most of them from the list of witnesses scheduled -- from the list scheduled for my own testimony. And now we have finally received your ruling last week, the refusal of nearly a thousand documents. And may I remind you in most cases, most trials before this Tribunal, the total number of documents put forward by both the Prosecution and the Defence teams never exceeded that, regardless of any possible or alleged formal areas by the lawyers, which is a separate procedure right now. For me, all of this is deeply unjust. Therefore, please allow me to say one thing, because I have been invited to speak sincerely. Had I, myself, passed an unjust decision like that, and you have all of that, the records, the rulings, it's all in the files, I stand by all of my decisions, even now I would have been greatly concerned. Fortunately, I didn't do any such thing. I did not make a single decision that resulted in such unfair consequences. That is why I'm entirely at peace with myself, awaiting the sentence. That is why I wrote the letter that I did last week, a letter that is not exactly in compliance with the procedure, although I do agree that procedure matters. I studied portions of your book, Judge Trechsel. I would not mind you applying any of what you wrote here, especially as regarded the rights of the accused. Unfortunately, that does not appear to be the case. You threw out all the video recordings of my interviews aired officially by the state television and watched by millions of people. Interestingly enough, we allowed the same person to do work based on those video recordings that actually produced the transcripts in the office of President Tudjman. This person is, as a matter of fact, still working in President Mesic's office. All of the presidential transcripts for which there was no audio recording were accepted; not just the audio recordings, but the video recordings. They are clean as a whistle and can be endorsed by the state television. Feel free to compare them to the video recordings tendered by the OTP, which you admitted, and the form in which they were submitted. Those recordings tell you what I said in public at the time relevant to the indictment. What can one possibly conclude? That you have no interest in knowing what I actually said during my public appearances at the time relevant to the indictment. How can you possibly stand by any decision that you are about to make. I simply fail to understand that. You refused as unauthentic the regulations from the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a member country of the UN, and all the while this Tribunal is supposed to bring peace and stability back to the region. You refused to admit documents, the official lists of municipalities, showing that, to all practical intents, all the municipalities did the same thing. All of these are documents important to understand the overall context. What I want to know is this: What, then, can possibly be used as documentary evidence if not, by definition, documents from Official Gazettes? I even said that in April 2007 in this very courtroom, when I opposed, in a general sense, the principle itself of documentary evidence, unless presented in a very restricted form. Nevertheless, the Prosecution was allowed to go ahead with that. What I want to have is the same sort of approach, even if the bar is raised even further up. Or, for example, you refused certain minutes from meetings of the HVO, corroborated by those involved in those meetings, while, on the other hand, you accepted the transcripts without any witnesses being put forward by the OTP. The objective of my Defence is to show and submit any minutes taken by any of the bodies that I chaired and any decisions taken there. This is the only way to have a proper foundation for a good and fair decision. There is one remark I would like to make. I fail to understand, based on what documents bearing a seal, referred to as the seal of Croatia's State Archive, are taken with no reservations at all as authentic, but not those presented by my Defence. Neither the HVO, as a provisional body of executive government, nor the Government of Herceg-Bosna, had any relation at all to that institution which was in a different country, nor, indeed, during an overview of all the files contained in that archive, does the word "Government of Herceg-Bosna" appear. You refused documents in relation to which those involved in the actual events confirmed their authenticity by their signatures; for example, the vice-president of the Republika Srpska, the director of a state television, and the security minister of that same country. Those aren't documents that would eventually decide the trial. These are perfectly ordinary documents, such as hundreds of others that have been admitted in this trial. There is no individual document in this type of trial -- that exists in this type of trial where the dominant factor is the power of various scenarios written about these or similar facts to actually convince anyone. I repeat, the one thing that I ask of you is to admit into evidence authentic documents that will help you to pass a just and fair decision. This is in the best interests of everyone, as I said in a letter, including the Prosecutor, bearing in mind the Prosecutor's mandate, in the interest of the international community and the victims alike, because take my word for it, the victims would not like to see convicted someone who is blameless. You, too, need authentic documents. Refuse any document that you believe to be unauthentic or useless, for example, because something has been sufficiently argued already. I will not be asking a single question about that. Nevertheless, documents have been thrown out or refused at this late stage for formal or unknown but certainly not essential reasons. These formal reasons are now being dealt with through a special procedure which provides you with room to do what is only logical. In principle, now is not the time to decide on their relevance, given the fact that you could still refuse all those documents and decide not to admit them at the end of trial. My last topic. Judge Antonetti says, and I believe that his intentions were good, last Thursday, that he understands that I may be desperate, that psychologically the situation is difficult and that's why I am not appearing at trial. You cannot have me face a situation like that, given the three hours of waiting today. A man with faith can never be desperate. Needless to say, no one likes to be in prison. I am disappointed, although I know how the world works and what it's like. That is no news to me. I am unafraid. I experienced the entire European history of the 19th and 20th centuries in a mere 10 years. As my own minister of the interior in the BH government, Jozo Leotar, used to say, who incidentally was killed in Sarajevo, and the killer was never found, I quote: "I have no room for fear left after everything that I've already been through." I do not seek your understanding or your mercy. I only seek what is no more than logical and just. I do understand that yours is not an easy task. In this trial, the indictment being what it is, 126.000 alleged rulings that you need to make, bearing in mind the responsibility that is incumbent upon you, believe me, I would always prefer to be an accused rather than a judge. You could commit errors. I'm no longer in a position to make any errors. Since most of us don't have the experience, believe me, there is no sensation of equanimity more beautiful or more complete than to feel blameless and yet be in prison. In these five months, in addition to reading the transcripts from the trial and anything else related to the trial, I had more time to spare than before. I'm not undergoing all these checks and transports every day. Perhaps you don't know this, but each and every day four men in uniform, such as our guards, would check us head to toe, including all of our cavities. I am now finishing the manuscripts for two of my new books. I also organised an installation -- an exhibition of pottery. I started playing music after 35 years. I'm setting up a band with my guards. Therefore, I'm not desperate, and I'm not shaken or, indeed, stirred. I have never taken a single pill throughout these five years. I am telling you this because it's been a long time since we last saw each other, and among other things, the Trial Chamber is supposed to take into account the overall situation of an accused. Nevertheless, now that I am speaking about this, allow me to say one thing that I do mind. I would mind if you considered me to be a criminal who would run away if provisionally released. Even when one is allowed to leave for a couple of days for purely documentary reasons, one is to remain under house arrest, regardless of any guarantees offered by a country that happens to be a member of the Security Council of the UN and NATO. You cannot consider me to be a criminal until I have been convicted. You don't have that right, and I don't want to know about any jurisprudence of any Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal. This is simply not to be found in any of the fundamental documents establishing this Tribunal. The presumption of innocence prevails and has the better overall of your bises, ters, and quaters. In the Prosecution's opinion, I constitute a risk in terms of escape, and humanitarian reasons are not sufficient for them. For example, I was not provisionally released for a week during the winter break. As you all know, my father died subsequently. I thank everyone for their compassion. I'll skip this portion. My Defence has been completed, and there is nothing that can be changed about it, nor indeed would I wish to change anything about it. Again, I impose no conditions, and I do not seek anything. My failure to appear here was not meant to exert pressure on anyone. It's just what I wrote. Please consider all documentary evidence. I've gone through all of it again just this last weekend, and I don't see anything problematic about it. I don't see anything that was not justified in keeping with your remarks; thousands of pages, very comprehensive, with all the dates, that the paragraphs of the indictment that this was in relation to, why a document was important, reasons for a document to be reviewed or reconsidered, how this was related to the indictment. And then in a particularly comprehensive annex, I stated the document's importance in relation to the paragraphs of the indictment. I also asked that you read the addendum to my statement. It is entirely up to you how you are going to treat this. You're professional Judges, you're not a jury. I'm prepared to by doing what I propose to do throughout this time to allow for a continuation of the trial and in this way be of assistance to this Trial Chamber. All I ask of you, I repeat, is to be given a chance to tender relevant evidence, even if the bar is set far higher up than in the case of the Prosecutor, evidence that might help you to make a good and just decision. I do not understand why you deprive yourselves of these documents that might help you to establish the truth. If that proves to be impossible, then my answer to your question about the character of this procedure is very explicit. Do not allow for me to lose my last illusion that this is, in fact, the case. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Prlic. I could just say, well, the Trial Chamber will deliberate and we'll give you our position later on, but I want to assume our own responsibility, and because of that I want to answer. As I told you earlier in the preamble, I'm very glad to see you back. Your departure a few months ago, and I said so at the time, seemed to be a disproportionate response to the problem at hand. Even if you could follow the trial from your cell, still it is best for you to be there. It's more useful for you, as well as for your co-accused. Secondly, in your statement we see that the main problem for you is the admission of documents. Now, on this issue, you know what my personal position has been. I stated it over and over again. I wrote a number of dissident opinions. I even wanted the Appeals Chamber to rule on the merits on the following question: When a Judge wants a document to be in the procedure, can a majority rule against it? The Appeals Chamber decided not to answer this question, saying that Trial Chamber decisions can only be made as a majority. So the question that I had raised was not answered by the Appeals Chamber. And because of this the Trial Chamber has admitted unanimously a number of documents and has also sometimes rejected a number of documents according to a majority rule, and it's always been the practice. Then, suddenly, we had the issue of the document you had written, could we admit it, "yes" or "no," and the Trial Chamber here issued a unanimous answer. We could not technically admit this document, even though this document could be easily reintroduced. And I can now deal about the problem of time. Your counsel and yourself complained a number of times for not having enough time. Let me remind you, Mr. Prlic, that the Trial Chamber had given you 95 hours to present your case. I can tell you that at the time, this was a great challenge for the Trial Chamber. In order to determine the time that you would be allotted, we had to take a great number of parameters into account. There is one parameter that we did take into account, which was the fact that you would testify. We really thought that you would come and testify, which is why we allotted you 95 hours, whereas the others only had 55. We believed that you were supposed to have 40 hours extra, compared to the others. But I remind you that the liability and the responsibility that you incur is exactly the same as your co-accused. But we believed that you were going to testify, which is why we allotted 95 hours to the presentation of your case. We were very surprised to see that you didn't testify, and in place of that you called other witnesses. This was your defence strategy. It's your problem, your business. But if you had testified, as you must have noticed, with Mr. Praljak's testimony, I would have put questions to you, just like I put questions to him. And thanks to that, I'm sure that we would have scanned the entire amount of questions possible. Maybe I would have asked questions for 12 hours, not 6 as with Mr. Praljak, but maybe 12 days, but you did not, so I was not in a position to put questions to you. Now, you telling us that you would ask for a disjunction of this case. You know that the Trial Chamber made a decision and the Appeals Chamber confirmed it, so it was absolutely impossible to disjoin this case, especially when there is an accused who is allegedly a member of a JCE. Technically, it was impossible, so the decision of the Trial Chamber was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. But you can, of course -- you mentioned this again, telling us that this for you was a problem, but I think that the problem was ruled on. The question of time was also an issue that was ruled on. Now, you say that you didn't have -- you weren't allotted enough time. You gave us a few examples. Very well, I'm not challenging the examples that you chose to give us. And now there's a new problem, the question related to your counsels, and you are providing us with a solution. Of course, the Trial Chamber will take a look at this solution. I cannot say what possible solution will be chosen. The Trial Chamber will have to deliberate on this and rule on this. I don't believe that I'm competent at the moment to say anything. We have to wait for deliberation to have a joint decision. But you know that I've always been in favour of allowing an accused to put questions. What you said actually is very much in line with my concerns. Then there's another issue, the fact of all of this work that you did, the thousands of pages that you worked on, and you feel that Judges just didn't even read it, just discarded it. It was discarded for technical reasons, that's true, but everything was read, and it is still technically possible to reintroduce this document maybe through a witness. So nothing has been decided once and for all regarding this issue. Let me tell you that the examination and cross-examination of Mr. Praljak can allow to readdress elements that are introduced and presented in your document, and this at any time. So to sum things up, I believe first that it is a good thing to have you with us, it's a good thing to be able to hear what you have to say. I note with great satisfaction, because I was a bit worried at one time, that psychologically you are doing well, you're following -- and you're able to follow this trial. Very good. Now, you talked about provisional release. Let's be clear on this point. Requests for provisional release while waiting for the end of the trial has been rejected unanimously by the Trial Chamber and confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. Then you also mentioned the pending request. You know that the Trial Chamber gave a favourable answer to this, but the Prosecutor is appealing this decision, and it's up to the Appeals Chamber to rule on this. So let's wait and see, serenely. But the Trial Chamber gave a favourable answer to your motion, and this is evidence that the Trial Chamber is using presumption of innocence to your benefit, and fully, fully so. I really want you to be absolutely sure of this. This is absolutely present in my mind, as well as in the mind of my fellow Judges. Otherwise, we would never have granted this motion. Now, regarding Rule 98 bis, you told us that you didn't really understand what had happened, but I'm sure that your counsel told you that it is an Anglo-Saxon procedure. Normally at this stage in the trial, you only look at the Prosecution case and Prosecution evidence and nothing else, you take look at the Defence case or the Defence exhibits, that's just the way it is. It was actually written in our decision, and in the decision on Rule 98 bis, what you said was not taken into account. The Trial Chamber only looked at the Prosecution exhibits and evidence, which is actually the spirit and the letter of the law regarding this Rule, anyway. And let me -- and the Appeals Chamber said in its ruling that this decision had no impact on any guilt or -- verdict of guilty or not guilty that could occur in the end. So that's for Rule 98 bis. But what's essential for the moment is to know whether you will take the floor later on, when we have -- for the rest of our witnesses, Mr. Praljak and Mr. Praljak's witnesses, and so forth, but we have to wait for the ADC to render its decision. They should do this within a month, and we will have enough time to issue a decision regarding this point while we're waiting for the answer from the ADC. This is what I wanted to say, Mr. Prlic, right away. This has not been thought out, you know, it's a very spontaneous response. I don't know if this is reassuring or concerning, as far as you are concerned. I don't know. But let me tell you, it's very important to have you here. I believe it's very important to have you here in the courtroom so you can listen to what's happening, so you can give advice to your counsels, notably when there are witnesses testifying, testifying either against you or for you. I mean, it's very important for you to be here in order to contribute to the manifestation of the truth. You reminded us that you were an advocate of this Tribunal, that you took part in the Rome Conference, and you've always been -- you've always said that you supported this Tribunal. Unfortunately, you end as an accused, and the Trial Chamber, using the indictment and using the elements presented by the Defence, will have to deliberate on all this and rule on your guilt or innocence. We're not there yet, anyway. We still have about a year's worth of work before we can actually end this trial, at least end the presentation of the cases. Then there will be, of course, some time for the drafting of the judgement. In a nutshell, this is all I had to say, Mr. Prlic. Mr. Karnavas, do you have anything to add? Otherwise, if not, we could continue with our questions, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Your Honour, because I don't want the record to reflect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I wonder if I may interrupt you, because I also would like to say a few words. And afterwards, of course, then you may rise. As the President explained at the beginning of his statement, of course, the Trial Chamber will deliberate and we are going to study the statements made by Mr. Karnavas and also Mr. Prlic, and definitely, as also the President used to say, as a reasonable judge, "juge raisonnable," we have to look in all, very seriously, all arguments which we have heard today. I take the liberty to say only a few words because my name was also mentioned by Mr. Prlic, and also because Judge -- not "Judge" but Maitre Karnavas has made a certain reference to the Trial Chamber's approach and how the Trial Chamber regards the work of the Defence. And here what I would like really to emphasise very categorically: This Chamber, and I'm sure that I speak for my fellow Judges, but of course they are invited to comment whatever I am going to say, we have always -- we are sticking to the very basic principles of our procedure, the very basic principles of the fail trial, and we are doing our best really to follow all those rules which are, inter alia, are also included into Judge Trechsel's book which was mentioned by Mr. Karnavas as well, and we do not want to depart from those principles in the future, as in no other time and in the forthcoming trial of the trial. Now, it is my first point. My second point is that Mr. Prlic mentioned that he doesn't want to have a spot of blemish on his Defence team, and I do share his concern, and I believe I may say, really with all firmness, that this Trial Chamber doesn't want to blemish -- to blame, rather, the team, of course not only Mr. Karnavas but the team as such, the co-counsel as such, as well, and therefore it is my final remark that we are not looking at the Defence team as, and I quote Mr. Karnavas "deceitful lawyers," and we do not regard them, again I quote Mr. Karnavas, "lawyers as sleazy lawyers." So no Damocles sword is being hung above your heads. Mr. Karnavas and the team, you may rest assured that this trial will be continued with all insistence on the well-accepted principles of international national criminal law, and we are going to do our best to see to it that this trial is to be concluded in this spirit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just two quick points of clarification, Mr. President, because I want the record to be very clear. When we were provided with the amount of hours ultimately that we would have, it was at that time that a decision was made for Mr. Prlic not to testify. We did not choose to call other witnesses in lieu of Dr. Prlic's testimony. Our problem was we couldn't have our cake and eat it, too, as it were. We couldn't have all the witnesses that we thought were necessary and Dr. Prlic take the entire amount of time. We couldn't have Dr. Prlic testify and then delete half of our witnesses, and we felt that we needed all of those witnesses in order to put on a complete defence. So I just wanted to make that very clear. So it wasn't as if we called others in order to fill in the gap. This was a full complement. And then we understood -- Ms. Tomanovic and I understood that the Appeals Chamber was unlikely to change the Trial Chamber's decision regarding time. Others appealed; we did not. We did not because we knew that this was a discretionary matter, and we decided that we would have to live by those hours and make the necessary adjustments. So adjustments were made, and as in any trial the situation is dynamic, you make changes as you go along. We made changes that we thought were necessary at the time, and unfortunately one of the problems was Mr. Prlic's work regarding Tomljanovich was not able to come before you either through his testimony or through him reading it, and that -- so I just wanted to put that -- make that very clear. And just secondly, just very briefly, the 98 bis, the motion for judgement of acquittal, I would agree with you that this is an Anglo-Saxon procedure, had it been kept the way it was meant to be kept initially. But since the Rules were amended, in my opinion, it's nothing more than a reconfirmation of the indictment when you don't consider anything that was presented. And, unfortunately, on the one hand, it is rather meaningless, to be very blunt, to have a 98 bis. I would just do away with it completely. It's a waste of judicial time and effort. On the other hand, the Appeals Chamber then turns around and says, Now that we've had the 98 bis judgement of acquittal, and nobody's been acquitted, now you are more of a security risk, and therefore the bar goes up with respect to other issues, such as provisional release for humanitarian reasons. So that's -- I just want to make it clear that the Rule, as it is today, is not Anglo-Saxon. I don't know what it is. And I would be the first one to say let's just get rid of it and save the time and energy and just go right into the Defence case after that. It would just save everybody time. Initially, it was meant that all of the evidence would be taken into consideration, if a judgement was, as in the Blagojevic, one-third of the case was eliminated, it wasn't appealed. So then we put forward a defence based on the two-thirds that remained. But be that as it may, I just wanted to clarify that point. And we appreciate the comments and the courtesy and the consideration provided by everyone from the Bench today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, would you like to take the floor on the fact that Mr. Prlic would like to put questions during this interim phase, after Mr. Praljak's testimony, maybe up until October, while we're waiting for a Trial Chamber decision regarding the opinion it asked from the ADC?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that on that, I would request -- I'd like to confer with my colleague, Mr. Scott, and perhaps others in the Office of the Prosecutor to see what the Office's position would be on that. And it's obviously not a terribly urgent matter, and I think it's something that we could come back to the Trial Chamber about at a later time. If I could add, however, I think that I can say that the Prosecution would oppose a suspension of the trial, which I know Mr. Karnavas has mentioned. And I know that there is disagreement among the Defence team about that, but the Prosecution position -- and I think at this particular stage procedurally, with one of the Defence teams cross-examining, perhaps one more cross-examination by the Pusic Defence team, and then moving into the Prosecution cross-examination, and then of course the summer recess beginning the week after next, I think procedurally we're in a safe zone, if I can put it that way, and that it's perhaps not an issue that would arise in any event over the next few days, and that would give us all time to consider what our position would be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I stated what I believe should be the case. However, I defer to my client. My client gives me instructions. My client did not categorically give me the permission to insist and thereby placing the Trial Chamber in some sort of a conundrum. I stated my position. I leave it to the Trial Chamber's discretion to decide what to do, whether to suspend or whether to allow Dr. Prlic, if it becomes necessary, to ask questions. But perhaps I wasn't as articulate as I could have been in stating that position. So we're not -- I am not, as his counsel, insisting on that. That is my position. I do tend to believe that no one should be representing themselves in court. I mean, that's -- we have that old adage, a lawyer who represents himself in court has a fool for a client. Now, that's not always the case, because I've seen people who represent themselves who do a better job than their lawyers. But we are concerned, but we leave it to Your Honours' discretion, and we are certainly not going against the wishes of our client. We defer to whatever Mr. Prlic wishes the outcome to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Chamber will hand down a decision on this issue. Yes, Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I didn't propose that I represent myself. This was not my idea, and it's not necessary to call a big legal procedure about it. My proposal was just that I will be public face of my defence in this period of time until this solution would emerge regarding this request to the chamber of lawyers next to this Tribunal. Just to be very clear on that, I am not going to take this possibility to represent myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic, in your proposal, to be very clear, from what I understood, you are going to want to ask questions, but I would like to know whether your counsels would also have the possibility to ask questions. Are you saying that during this time-frame, you will be the only one to be able to ask questions? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: The questions would be asked by me, or if I decide, it would be asked by someone from my team whom I authorise to do that, so this is not a big deal. But frankly speaking, I don't expect that any question is going to be put, but we'll see. I don't want to say no before such a situation emerged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic, let's just assume for one moment that in a few minutes the counsel of Mr. Coric takes the floor and talks about the HVO authorities and of yourself, and then Mr. Praljak will answer the questions, and at that juncture you feel that you would like to ask some clarification to Mr. Praljak, but at the same time Counsel Karnavas says, Well, actually, I would also like to ask a question. At that point, should Mr. Karnavas ask for your authorisation before he can take the floor and ask a question? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I'm not lawyer. I used to be diplomat. There is one rule in diplomacy. Never ask a hypothetical question. I don't know how to answer on that, but basically I would be asking -- I'm not able to now to say what is going to happen, but we just want to be clear that before dissolution of that, I understand position of my attorney. He doesn't want to be this public face without resolving this issue. So my attempt is just to find a solution, to be part of solution, not to make a problem of that. And let's not make a problem by not -- by trying to find a way how it's not going to function in such and such way. Let's think about that constructively. This is my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Prlic, we certainly appreciate your cooperative attitude. I just think perhaps the matter is not yet entirely clear. Do we understand, Mr. Karnavas, Ms. Tomanovic, that you will immediately, from this moment, cease to act in the courtroom on behalf of your client? Was that what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what I am saying is from this moment on until this matter is cleared, Dr. Prlic will be asking the questions, and this is in order to ensure that if Dr. Prlic says something or makes a representation, that it is accepted. Given -- as I noted before, given what we've read and how we've read it, and we've analysed it and tore it apart, we saw the forms of the questions, we saw some things that we thought were some insinuations, we believe that we are essentially hurting his case, not helping his case, and that is our concern. The moment I make a representation, if the Trial Chamber does not have confidence in me being a truthful advocate, that's the moment that I no longer belong in the case. And at this moment, at least there are allegations of truthfulness and deceitfulness, as we see them, and we want to make sure that this matter is cleared so then we can move on, because we are of the opinion that we did nothing wrong, we followed instructions given to us, we consulted with our client in advance. We provided the Trial Chamber what we believed was the entire truth. The Trial Chamber, on the other hand, said that we were content to just give vague answers. Well, when you look at it, cryptically what the Trial Chamber is saying is, we lied, to put it bluntly. So if that's the case, I'm concerned that when I stand up and I make an objection or I put -- make a representation, the Trial Chamber has less confidence in me. If you may recall, Judge Trechsel, when another accused made references about me and there was no reaction, I responded publicly in a very aggressive manner. Why? Because I felt that at that point in time, either the gentleman should put up or shut up. He should either demonstrate or he should be reprimanded. And that's why -- and my cause for reacting was that I believe that by not reacting, the impression was that the representation being made by the gentleman, the accused in the other case, were true, accurate, and complete. And so we take this very seriously, I can assure you. I spent the weekend consulting with lawyers, and I'm prepared to fly in experts, if necessary, to resolve this issue, because I take my professional responsibilities quite seriously. Now, I may be very aggressive in court. It may not be up to everyone's style. But when it comes to ethics, I know where the line is, and I certainly don't cross it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is not actually what I wanted to discuss, and I do not wish to discuss it now, of course, it would be, I think, improper. But I would like to know what your attitude from now on, until this matter is closed, will be. Will you continue to be in the courtroom? Will you continue, as the case may be, to make objections, for instance, which is the typical lawyer's work? And Mr. Prlic has just said that he's not a lawyer. Or will you actually withdraw and not be present? It would be helpful to know what we have to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, no one is withdrawing from the case. I cannot withdraw without permission, one, from the Trial Chamber and, two, from the Registry, most importantly. I think that's pretty established case law in this Tribunal. You know, I was the one that established it in another case, in fact, with a client insisting on me withdrawing and I was not -- and it was Ms. Tomanovic and I remained in the case throughout. So we're not withdrawing. Does that mean that both of us will be in the proceedings the entire time? The answer to that is "no," and the reason for that is as this case is rather complicated and there are other things that need to be done, when one of us is not in here it's because we're either working on other matters related to the case. When both of us are here, it's because we feel that it is most necessary, because we are in a process, I can assure you -- I don't think it's a major secret, but we are in the process at this moment of -- the early stages of looking and organising ourselves for the final brief. So we are not withdrawing, I can assure you. Dr. Prlic is not going to be left to dangle in the wind without legal protection. I can assure you of that. But -- and for the purposes of the Court, Dr. Prlic had a suggestion. I think this is his way of trying to assist his counsel in this hour of need, because we feel that we are damaging his case, and therefore he's stepping up to the plate to take over any questioning in court, if necessary, while we assist him and continue to assist him in our full capacity as his lawyers, counsel and co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I may be very naive, and I don't know, Mr. Karnavas, but my -- my question is very simple. I was not thinking of a withdrawal from the case at all, because what you told us is not news to me. The question is actually: Are you going to be represented, one, the other, or both, in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you will be perhaps acting for Mr. Prlic when you think an objection must be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I act whenever I think anybody needs assistance on the Defence side, to be honest with you. That's my nature. I've even done that when I wasn't in the courtroom, if I was sitting in the back, in the audience. I've always believed that accused deserve -- if they need help, I'm willing to pitch in. So if I -- but having said that, we don't believe, at this stage of the proceedings, in light of what is happening in the courtroom right now, that we need to be active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you are going to go on representing Mr. Prlic a little, but not for questioning? Is that the result?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not a little. I can assure you, we work six, seven days a week, Your Honour, and that's the work that -- we will continue to work that. We will continue. In the courtroom, Dr. Prlic wishes to be a more active player henceforward, and I think this is -- this is good. Now, to the extent if, for instance, it becomes necessary for us to step in, we will step in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Then practically what's going to happen is that 1D will become Praljak-ised, it will be more or less what Mr. Praljak has been doing so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I guess you could say that. You may recall when we first -- the motion, we were the team that filed the motion, actually, to allow accused to ask questions, in addition to their lawyers. But the answer is "yes." My reaction, to be very frank, I would like the proceedings to be stop, because I do think that this cloud needs to be lifted. My client does not want under any circumstances for the proceedings to stop, and so -- and he's suggesting that he assist while, you know -- while the proceedings continue. And, of course, this is his case, it is his skin, and he's entitled to assist in his own defence, so he wishes at this point to be a more active participant in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This question is before the Chamber now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So it will be deliberated. I think now we have gained some clarity on what we have to expect from --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise for not being as clear as I could have been. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You certainly did your best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, in order for me to understand properly, you are going to carry on assisting Dr. Prlic, and if Dr. Prlic feels that he should ask questions, he will. If you feel that you would like to raise an objection, you will also take the floor because you're counsel. So this is very clear as far as we are concerned. Well, actually, as far as I'm concerned. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, each of Your Honours. My name is Ken Scott, and I appear for the Prosecution sometimes. Your Honour, I think what's been demonstrated quite clearly in the last few minutes, that -- this hearing, with the greatest of respect, has turned into largely a proceeding of everyone thinking out loud. Various things have been said. They change from minute to minute. In response to Judge Trechsel's questions, things develop further, things are clarified, not clarified. It's very likely, Your Honour, that no matter what happens in this situation, no matter what the Chamber rules, there will likely be an appeal by one party or another. This is not a matter that lends itself to off-the-cuff, unpremeditated thinking or deliberation. As, Your Honour Mr. President [Realtime transcript read in error "President Putin"] you said a few moments ago, everyone in this proceeding except for Mr. Prlic and Mr. Karnavas who, with great respect, have obviously given the matter great thought in advance of coming here day, but neither the Chamber has had a chance prior to the last few minutes to consider these matters, nor the Prosecution. We are all essentially making unconsidered comments at this time, except for Mr. Prlic and Mr. Karnavas. The Chamber has said several times it will expect to rule. We understand, of course, that in all these matters, the Prosecution -- the Chamber will not rule until the Prosecution's had a full opportunity -- after a fair opportunity to consider these matters, which has just now been raised now for the first time, to prepare a timely written response, and in fact we would suggest, Your Honour, given the seriousness of the matters raised, given the seriousness of a need to make a record for appeal, that Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Prlic, if they deem it necessary, both individually to make written submissions as exactly to what it is how they propose to proceed, because, again, just as Judge Trechsel was indicating a moment ago, we're now dealing with a moving target. The rules are going to be this one day, the rules are going to be this another day. That is not a court of law. A court of law does not make up the rules as we go. There are rules that apply every day in advance that all the parties can live by and predict and prepare their behaviour accordingly. So, Your Honour, the Prosecution's position on this, and our request at this time, is that before anything further is done, written submissions be made by Mr. Karnavas and by Mr. Prlic, if necessary, the two of them, that they outline their positions very clearly in writing, that the Prosecution, under the Rules, has a fair opportunity to respond to those submissions in writing, and then, of course, the Chamber will be better postured to make a reasoned decision. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will deliberate on this motion. A small correction in the transcript. Page 75, line 2, I'm not yet President Putin. I don't know, there is something on the record that is strange. We'll now break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to hand down an oral order regarding the submissions. The Chamber is asking the parties to send written submissions to the Chamber, and the Chamber will ask the Prlic Defence to submit the written submission by Wednesday, at the latest, and is asking the Prosecutor and other Defence teams to also submit their written suggestions by Monday, 9.00, 9.00 a.m., at the latest. Mr. Karnavas will send us his written submission before Wednesday, and the Prosecutor and the other Defence teams will have until Monday, 9.00 a.m., to make suggestions before us, and this is Monday, 9.00 a.m., once again. So I believe everything is clear, and I'm going to give the floor to Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak into the microphone, please. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] We're going to move on to the second binder, and it says "Binder 2." So I hope you'll be able to find it, and let's start off with document P00309.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this is a document which is already an exhibit, as my colleague Ms. Alaburic has already told you, and she put it to you during her cross-examination. It is a mandatory directive on the application of current regulations and possible pronouncement of final sanctions for acts committed against the armed forces. This directive was passed by the head of the Defence Department, at the proposal, as it says at the top, of the president of the judiciary, and I'd like us to focus on the crimes listed, crimes against the armed forces. Among the crimes listed there, the first crime is: "Failure and refusal to carry out orders." And the term of imprisonment there which can be prescribed is from three months to ten years. Can you see that, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Before I go on with my questions, I'd just like to mention, to avoid all misunderstanding, is that I'm going to use the word "zapovjednik," "commander." When I say "zap ovjednik," I don't have any single commander in mind or the senior commander of the army, but I have in mind commanders from the level of squads and then up the structure. Do you agree with me, Mr. Praljak, that carrying out orders is the basis for discipline in every army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I would like to come back on this document. I wanted to ask you a question the first time around we looked at this document, but because we didn't have a lot of time I decided to not ask you the question then. But since Ms. Tomic is touching upon this, I'll seize this opportunity. Please correct me if I'm mistaken, but this document talks about the articles of the former Penal Code or Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia. These are articles from the former Yugoslavia, normative instruments, and you can see -- it can't have failed to your attention that Article 226 is also added with a comment. It says that in peacetime, imprisonment sentence can be handed down, but in wartime it can go up to death penalty. So this is very good, nothing to add to that. However, there is something missing, I believe. When you read the text, you have the feeling that it only applies to acts committed against armed forces of the HZ-HB, so I put myself in the shoes of a private who hasn't done a lot of studies and who is, however, able to read, and say, Okay, this will apply if an act is committed against myself or against my fellow privates. However, if they are acts committed the against the ABiH, there is nothing. So what is your take on this? Is it a mistake by the drafters or was that done on purpose, or did this fail to the attention of the lawmakers of the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a mistake, or omission, rather, because it says the -- for example, the federal law, et cetera, et cetera, the federal law that applied to the Yugoslav People's Army. And so apart from the true desire on the part of Mr. Stojic, who signed this directive, and the opinion of the judge who probably helped him or, rather, the lawyer who helped him draft it, this is applicable to the Yugoslav People's Army that existed during Tito's day and in some army that exists when a state exists, in the full sense of the word "state," as a legal state, a lawful state, and so on. So not only as far as the HVO is concerned and the BH Army is concerned, but this was not applicable even in the Yugoslav People's Army during the two years, because even before -- or, rather, at the beginning of the armed conflict, or, rather, the JNA's attack on Croatia, a large number of officers from the JNA left, senior officers as well, and soldiers alike, they fled, a large number of Muslims fled, too, and a large number of Serbs, for that matter, dozens of thousands of Serbs. Young men from Serbia who were military recruits left and went abroad. Anybody who had any money or had anybody abroad did so, escaped. So the whole system collapsed; not only the HZ-HB, but Yugoslavia collapsed. So that apart from the very good wishes to do something along these lines, to be quite frank, from start to finish this was completely unrealistic. You could not put this into practice at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, my previous question, and you answered in the affirmative, was that every army is based on the soldiers carrying out orders. Now, my next question is this: A commander who has issued an order is the person who knows that his subordinate refused to carry that order out or chose to ignore the order; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at the next document, which is P00293, and they are the rules governing military disciplinary measures. And let's look at Article 3 of the rules of military discipline. In Article 3, we see stipulated what is considered violations of the military rules, apart from the definition of the violation itself, and let's look at point 7, which says: "Punishable actions for which proceedings are initiated ex officio." Tell me, please, Mr. Praljak, are you acquainted with that provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That the commission of a criminal act would come under military disciplinary measures, no, I can't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm going to make an additional comment, but could -- I think one of the Judge's microphone is on, because it creates a noise in the courtroom. Thank you. Now, Mr. Praljak, I'm going to be quite frank with you. Until Ms. Alaburic cross-examined you, I wasn't going to deal with rules and regulations, and I wasn't going to ask you about that, because during the examination-in-chief you said that you didn't have time to read any rules, nor did you read them, nor are you informed of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In part, the essential parts which had to do with the functioning. But -- that I studied them, no, I did not, I didn't do that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: However, you did comment on some rules and regulations in response to Ms. Alaburic, so I'm only going to address those same rules. And one of these sets of rules are the rules on military discipline that we're looking at now. Now, let's look at Article 8. We saw that criminal acts come under military discipline, and in Article 8 -- may we have Article 8 on our screens, please, and the last two sentences there, where it says: "If a criminal act," and here the Croatian term is the same, "the perpetrator can be responsible before military disciplinary courts if this is required by the special interests of the service. The procedure before a military disciplinary court evolves regardless of the outcome of the penal proceedings." Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at Article 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand this, if I can be quite frank. I don't understand what you've just read out and what it means. How can a criminal act be dealt with by military disciplinary courts and penal proceedings? I don't understand any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this is a very complex issue; I realise that. And this may have consequences on Article 7(3) of the Statute. Since you were the commander of the HVO and you know that officers can hand down disciplinary rulings and sentences; for instance, the brigade commander can say to his soldiers, You are going to be sent to prison for ten days as a disciplinary measure because you did not show respect to your superiors, so he will be in a military confinement for ten days as per the sentence, and as the text states, and, General Praljak, there are also disciplinary sanctions that are no longer the remit of the brigade commander, but of a higher disciplinary entity, namely, the disciplinary tribunal or court, hence your query. You say, Well, if a crime has been committed, why should there be a disciplinary sanction, and you are very right, because when we deal with crimes, if you just said to a soldier, You have killed a civilian, and therefore you are going to be sent to prison for 15 days, this would be an outrage, and this is why the prosecutor gets to know the matter; hence, for a brigade commander to be fully aware of what is in his own responsibility or remit and what is the remit of the military prosecutor. As HVO commander, were you faced with this sort of situation where you did not know whether the sanction or the recourse was of your remit? Say, for instance, a soldier had stolen a car, was that a disciplinary sanction or should it be the remit of the military prosecutor? Were you faced with this sort of situation, and if that is the case, how did you solve it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I did find myself in situations like that, and it was very clear to me. Disciplinary measures have to do with offences, so if a soldier got drunk or committed some minor offence or misdemeanor, or if he wasn't performing his duty in the trenches properly, that kind of thing. But I was quite clear on the fact that theft and everything above theft, crimes above theft, were criminal acts and, therefore, needed to be reported so that criminal proceedings could be initiated. On one occasion, for example, in Sunja I captured a soldier -- or a soldier was brought to me who had stolen something. I escorted him to the prison in Sisak, and then from my own money I paid for defence counsel to defend him. So I'm not a layman. I knew the procedure. Of course, I'm not an expert, but I'm not a complete layman either. So I took him into custody, took him to the prison there, and then I paid defence counsel to defend him, to represent him. So all criminal acts are dealt with by the courts. They can't be dealt with by commanders, not even the commander of the Main Staff, the chief of the Main Staff. They can't get involved in anything that the law sees as a criminal act, starting with theft, or brawls, or grievous bodily harm, where grievous bodily harm was inflicted, and so on. If they just have a brawl in a bar, that's a different matter, without any consequences. Then, disciplinary measures could be applied, but otherwise not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another example that might give you some clarification. Let's assume that you realise that a soldier is wearing a Swiss watch. In his pocket, he has some Hungarian delicatessen, and then he's wearing a jacket from a French designer, and you're asking him, Where does it come from, and he says, It's war booty, what do you decide? Is it a disciplinary sanction or will it be the jurisdiction of a military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That of a military prosecutor. He can't keep this war booty by just seizing it. That is theft. That's how the offence should be classified. And as was the case with the policeman in Ljubuski, would report him. I would sit down to it, I would say, Such and such a person did this or did that, ranging from that policeman to anyone at all, if the elements are there. I reported such cases. This is not a disciplinary measure. It's not about that. This is an offence. It's not war booty. War booty, when it comes to weapons and other such items, must be declared. If a soldier comes across something like this in an abandoned house or something like that, he has to declare this to the brigade, to the military police, to the SIS, or indeed his own commander, and then the commander would have to make a note and pass this along. We cannot just have war booty by allowing individuals to take whatever they like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned friend Dijana could please forgive me, page 81, one thing that was not recorded was the answer by General Praljak when he was speaking about disciplinary courts. The last thing that was recorded was that he said he didn't understand this, but the general also says: "I'm not sure if that even existed." If we listen to the tape, we can check that very easily, but I don't want it to go unrecorded. And then we could ask the general whether he said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as a matter of fact, I know that. There was simply no lawyers anywhere around, and that's why military disciplinary courts did not operate. I'm not sure if that decision was taken or not, but there weren't any lawyers who could work on that. How do you make a decision? There were no lawyers. They had a hard time setting up the military criminal courts, or whatever that was called, to the extent that they did. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would like to press on for another couple of minutes with this same issue that I started off with. What happens when, at the same time, we have something that is a disciplinary infraction which also amounts to an offence? The last thing I asked was to look at Article 14, paragraph 4 which reads: "The Statue of Limitations on a disciplinary infraction which also constitutes an offence takes effect at the same time as the Statue of Limitations in relation to an offence." Are you aware of this, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, let's move on to Article 29. Article 29 reads: "When an authorised official assesses that there has been an infraction of military discipline leading to the commission of an offence, the case shall be handed over to an authorised prosecutor through official channels. If it is believed to be in the interests of the service, the officer shall undertake measures to initiate disciplinary proceedings in this regard." Were you aware of this, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, madam. I took a different approach. When there was a disciplinary procedure, whenever an offence was committed, this would be handled by a court, or at least that's what I thought at the time. Regardless of this paragraph, I think that is still the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph in that same article: "When a violation of military discipline represents a punishable act against the armed forces which, pursuant to the Penal Code, is subject to disciplinary proceedings, the superior officer shall transfer the case to the officer authorised to decide on the breach of discipline." Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I don't understand this. If there is an infraction of military discipline that constitutes a criminal offence, then it's a criminal offence; right? I fail to fathom this, to be perfectly frank. And then we don't have disciplinary proceedings or steps because we are dealing with a criminal offence, and this is something that should be handled by a court. I simply fail to understand how a disciplinary infraction might have the features of a criminal offence and then be treated as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm in no position to furnish any explanations or clarifications here. I'm just trying to shed light on what actually applied at the time, what regulations, and I'm trying to work through this with you in a bid to learn whether you knew about some things or not, or maybe you were uninformed on a number of issues. Had you been properly informed, you would have taken different steps, as opposed to the ones you did. That is the intention of my cross-examination. I can't change the regulations that once applied and were in force. At this point in time, it is quite irrelevant whether you or I find them logical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not have acted differently even if I had been fully aware of all these. Even if I had been fully aware of this entire document, a disciplinary procedure would have still constituted a disciplinary procedure, and a criminal offence would always have remained a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us now look at Article 69, which reads: "When a disciplinary infraction is committed by the same act as the criminal offence --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Article 69, there is Article 63 that could allow you, General Praljak, to answer some of your queries. Do you see Article 63? It states that if, during the investigation, another type of proceedings should be launched, then the officer will decide to refer the case to the relevant authority. So it is possible for an officer to make a mistake and to launch an investigation of a disciplinary nature, and then eventually they realise that it should be the jurisdiction of a military disciplinary court. So do you think that Article 63 could solve this problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am being perfectly clear, speaking about what I did and what I said to my own officers. Discipline is discipline. You shall punish anything that amounts to a criminal offence. Will you report this, and criminal proceedings will be initiated. There you go. Now, as to whether this article sheds any light on that, that is a legal issue for you to deal with. What I can say is what my position was when I led the soldiers and what I said to my officers. Discipline to the extent that it is possible. I'm talking about intentions here. Anything that constituted a criminal offence should be handled by a court. It wasn't down to officers to rule on anyone's guilt whenever a criminal offence was committed. At any rate, international law, which is something that I try to hammer into the heads of each of Croatia's and HVO's soldiers, and I must say that each and every soldier at one point or another was familiarised with the provisions of International Humanitarian Law or Law of War, they all knew that there were a number of provisions -- standards that had to be met to have a fair trial once they ended up facing a trial chamber. There are 16 or 17 paragraphs there, actually; the public nature of the trial, the right to a defence, and so on and so forth. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Article 69, this is the last article on this topic. Article 69 reads: "When a disciplinary offence has been committed in the course of the punishable action, the officer authorised to bring the offender before the military disciplinary court shall decide whether the service's special interests require that the offender also be brought before the military disciplinary court for the disciplinary offence. "If service interests do not require that the offender be brought before the military disciplinary court, the officer, as described in paragraph 1 of this Article, shall suspend the disciplinary proceedings and bring the punishable action to the authorised public prosecutor." Were you aware of this, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither was I aware of this, nor, indeed, do I understand it. This is outside my ken.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next document, please, 3D03027. This is a document produced by Colonel Blaskic, dated the 31st of August, 1993. The document was sent to the HVO Main Staff, the Citluk Forward Command Post. The document reads: "Report," and then I'll go on to read certain portions; not all of the names, though. That will take too long. But where it says: "On the 13th of August, 1993, I launched a disciplinary investigation against," and then a list of names, "who on the 10th of August, 1993, broke into the offices of the civilian police, disarmed the policemen there, and took their weapons and vehicles. "Once the investigation was completed, the following steps were taken: "Criminal reports for violent behaviour, as described in Article 204, paragraph 2, of the adopted KZ SR BH were filed ...," and then a list of perpetrators? Item 2: "Ranko Milicevic, the deputy commander, was relieved of his duties." General Praljak, I wish to ask you the following. I'm slightly confused after all your answers, saying that you didn't know that a disciplinary infraction might have continue constituted a crime and what happened next. I'm somewhat confused, but please tell me if you agree with me that this document illustrates precisely a situation of that kind, what I described a while ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones not being used please be switched off. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And the authorised officer decided that there should be disciplinary measures taken relieving the officer of his duties? Do you agree with me? This is an example that best illustrates this kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, madam, he was relieved of his duties. But a person who is being charged with something cannot retain his or her position. It would have been illogical for them to say, And because of this, another 30 days in prison. That was my understanding of the previous "..." Obviously, if there is a criminal procedure on the way against someone, that person cannot remain in his position as the commander of the HVO or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: That, indeed, is my understanding as well. Let us please briefly go back to P0029, the disciplinary "..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the example chosen probably illustrates the difficulty of the thing. Colonel Blaskic is reporting to the headquarters. He's reporting on the behaviour of a person who disarmed the policemen. And here we have Article 204 that is mentioned, but when you look at Article 204, it is disobeying an order. Maybe, after all, this soldier was ordered not to take into account the civilian police, but here the civilian policemen are disarmed and their weapons and vehicles are taken away from them. It could very well be a military action dealing with the civilian police or it could be -- it could just be plain theft. So you could really have a double reading of the case. If the private disobeyed an order, then this can come under the jurisdiction of a disciplinary sanction because this order was not supposed to deal with the civilian policeman and actually did. But if he just wanted to steal the car and the weapons, then this is criminal conduct. It's different. Were you ever confronted with this kind of situation where you could have a double reading of the event? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, just a minute. I think there's been some confusion. Judge Antonetti, Article 204 is not from the military discipline rules. It's from the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear counsel because two speakers were overlapping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what I'm saying. Disobedience is on P0034, Article 204. This isn't what I'm saying, Ms. Tomic. Normally, I don't make mistake. I am saying that Article 204 deals -- is an article that we have in document P00-309, and that Article 204 deals with disobeying an order, punishable by up to a three-year prison sentence. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what you are reading from P00309 is an excerpt from the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia which applied throughout the territory. What I was reading from, Colonel Blaskic's document, is from the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which also applied. In the former Yugoslavia, there was the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia which applied throughout all of the republics, regulating one set of issues, and then some other issues were regulated by the criminal codes of each of the respective republics. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, both criminal codes applied before the war and during the war. The one that I read from, 204, is from the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we are talking about violent behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Ms. Tomic, but I'm absolutely sure that Article 204 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina is exactly the same one as the one we would have for the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. It's the same Article, but that's not where the problem lies. Mr. Praljak, when a military commander is confronted with this kind of situation, he doesn't know whether an order was not correctly abided by or whether it isn't actually an offence, isn't there a doubt there as to what sanction needs to be given, whether it's up to the military courts to be seized or whether it is up to the commander to actually sanction the soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. Colonel Blaskic knows perfectly well that these five persons broke into the premises of the civilian police, disarming police officers and seizing weapons and vehicles. Had he issued this order for whatever reason, obstruction of a military action and so on and so forth, then because of classified information having been given away, he would have had those military policemen prosecuted. Nevertheless, they did this at their own initiative, quite obviously, so he was taking some specific and clear steps there. In a legal sense, this is both logical and fair. He returns the goods that were seized, relieves of his duties the commander of the 3rd Battalion, and hands over the entire case to the military judicial authorities; the prosecutor, more specifically. It would strike me as counter-intuitive for me for him to say here that he would punish Ranko Milicevic by imposing a punishment of 20 days in the military remand prison. He should be prosecuted for violent behaviour for a criminal offence that he committed, and the sentence was likely to be much more considerable in that case. That was what I failed to understand about those paragraphs. What is a procedure that is both disciplinary and criminal at the same time? That wasn't clear. But this one is crystal clear. They report that he's dispatched to the Main Staff. There is nothing to add. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could counsel please speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this got completely lost. You have to go three steps back and then start again. If you look at the transcript, there's nothing here. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, it appears that the interpreters were not -- my question was what the intention was of Mr. Blaskic when he took these steps as described in this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blaskic did the right thing. In a legal sense, in the military sense, this was logical. He did exactly what a commander would have been expected to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like us now to take a look at the military disciplinary rules once again, please, for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic has asked: What were the motives of General Blaskic? The answer was: "He did the right thing," but that is not really an answer to that question. But it's a question that asks for speculation, and maybe, therefore, you say, How should I know what was the scope of Mr. Blaskic's action. But you are expected to answer this, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document shows what the motive was, and the motive was to punish the person who violated the law. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise. Judge Trechsel is quite right. I asked the question in one way and then I was interrupted, so I asked it in another way. So this was because of technical reasons. But let's go back to P000293, the Rules on Military Discipline, and we can look at Article 24 for my next question. Let's look at Article 24, which says that the commanders of units or, rather, institutions -- the commanders of garrisons, and then it goes on to list who the garrison commanders are, pronounce disciplinary measures for other perpetrators that are not in their organic composition, if they are necessary in order to preserve law and order and discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed about that? And let me tell you straight away that I interpret this in the following way: When a commander commands units, in the operational sense, which are not his own units but find themselves under his command, because of law, order, and discipline, for example, up at the front, is authorised to exercise disciplinary measures -- to take disciplinary measures against them. Is that how you understood this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably you understand this better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you -- did you know about this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was not informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now let's go forward and look at P -- 5D04039. 5D04039 is the document number. This a document from the commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, Mr. Pasko Ljubicic. This is before your time, the 8th of July, 1993, before you took up your duties, but I'll show you the document and put it to you nonetheless. It is sent to the brigade, HVO Bobovac Brigade from Vares, to the commander, Emil Harah, in person. Pasko Ljubicic says the following in this document: "Members of the military police, according to orders issued so far in the sense of command, are subordinated exclusively to the commanders of the brigades in their zone of responsibility. Military police units must comply with the mentioned order. Each member of the military units who oppose your orders or do not carry them out should be punished by you, just like other soldiers in your unit. According to your judgement, you have the right to exclude persons from the military police unit whom you consider to have a negative influence." Tell me now, Mr. Praljak, did you know of situations like this, and does this document reflect the situation as described in Article 24 that we saw a moment ago linked to the composition of the units and command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, partially, and let me explain this. In March, I was in Central Bosnia, and at the time Mr. Blaskic had already very clearly assumed, just like all his services, that the situation would come to a head with the BH Army and that a conflict would break out, or, rather, that the BH Army would launch an attack. That was his assumption and his forecast. And going to Central Bosnia already at that time meant a great risk for every HVO member, it was risky, because apart from the regular BH Army check-points, if I can call them that, there were those check-points that had been set up by the man Paraga, for example, where he could kill you without giving it a second thought. So when I, in March 1993, went up there, Blaskic asked me that because of the foreseeable future, I should discuss the return with Mate Boban and the rest, and that because of the specific position that Central Bosnia had, Vares and all the other places, that two things be enabled, that he be enabled to do two things: first of all, to appoint commanders, which otherwise was not the case because there was no communication and he could not communicate either with Petkovic, or Stojic, or anybody else; and, secondly, that he be allowed to use the military police, because if there was an attack, he could not go through the lengthy procedure of sending in a request and then be given permission to deploy the military police. By that time, he could have lost a whole series of positions that he held. Now, after my return, I certainly talked to Mate Boban and conveyed this to him, and I considered this to be a good idea. I also talked to General Petkovic, who considered it to be a good idea. I don't know if I discussed it with Mr. Stojic. I don't want to venture into that. But, anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: General Praljak, I wonder, if I may, interrupt you, because we are going to finish in ten minutes and two of us here would also like to ask questions. But if you have something very important to say, tell us in the next two minutes, and then we will proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
